los.lo: List the international system of units of measurement (SI) for mass, acceleration, weight, velocity, energy, density, temperature, pressure, force, wing loading, and power.
los.title: SI units
los.html:
Theory & physics

The exam uses SI units: mass in kg, acceleration in m/s², force and weight in newtons (N = kg·m/s²), velocity in m/s, energy in joules (J = N·m), power in watts (W = J/s), density in kg/m³, temperature in kelvin, pressure in pascals (Pa = N/m²) and wing loading in N/m².

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Weight is a force, so it is in newtons, not kg.
  • Wing loading has the same unit as pressure: N/m².
  • Gas-law temperatures are always in kelvin (15 °C = 288 K).

los.lo: Define ‘mass’, ‘force’, ‘acceleration’, and ‘weight’.
los.title: Mass, force, acceleration and weight
los.html:
Theory & physics

Mass is the amount of matter in a body and its resistance to acceleration (inertia); it is the same everywhere. A force changes a body's state of rest or motion. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, in speed or direction. Weight is the force of gravity on a mass: W = m × g, with g ≈ 9.81 m/s².

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Mass does not change with altitude or location; weight does (slightly).
  • A change of direction at constant speed is still an acceleration.
  • 70 000 kg × 9.81 ≈ 687 kN.

los.lo: State and interpret Newton’s three laws of motion.
los.title: Newton's laws
los.html:
Theory & physics

1st law: a body stays at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless a resultant force acts. 2nd law: F = m × a: a resultant force gives an acceleration in its direction. 3rd law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction: a wing pushes air down and is pushed up; a propeller pushes air back and is pushed forward.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Steady, straight and level flight = zero resultant force (1st law), not "lift greater than weight".
  • A turn at constant speed needs a resultant force towards the centre (2nd law).
  • Lift and thrust are explained by the 3rd law reaction on the air.

los.lo: Explain air density.
los.title: Air density
los.html:
Theory & physics

Air density (ρ) is the mass of air per unit volume: 1.225 kg/m³ at ISA sea level. All aerodynamic forces are proportional to it, because a wing makes its force by changing the momentum of the air it meets.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Lower density means less lift and drag at the same TAS and angle of attack.
  • ISA sea-level density: 1.225 kg/m³.

los.lo: List the atmospheric properties that effect air density.
los.title: What affects air density
los.html:
Theory & physics

Density depends on pressure, temperature and humidity.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Humid air is less dense than dry air (water vapour is lighter than N₂ and O₂).
  • "Hot, high and humid" = lowest density = poorest performance.

los.lo: Explain how temperature and pressure changes affect air density.
los.title: Temperature, pressure and density
los.html:
Theory & physics

Higher pressure packs more molecules into a volume, so density rises with pressure; higher temperature spreads them out, so density falls with temperature. In a climb pressure falls faster than temperature, so density falls with altitude: about half its sea-level value at 22 000 ft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Climbing: both p and T fall, but the pressure effect wins, so ρ decreases.
  • Warmer than ISA at the same pressure altitude = lower density.

los.lo: Define ‘static pressure’.
los.title: Static pressure
los.html:
Theory & physics

Static pressure (p) is the pressure the air exerts on a surface moving with it, acting equally in all directions. It is the pressure of the undisturbed atmosphere, sensed by the static ports.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Static pressure exists whether the air moves or not.
  • It acts in all directions; dynamic pressure only appears when flow is brought to rest.

los.lo: Define ‘dynamic pressure’.
los.title: Dynamic pressure
los.html:
Theory & physics

Dynamic pressure (q) is the extra pressure the air would exert if brought to rest: the kinetic energy of the flow per unit volume.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • It is a pressure "from motion" only: zero when the aircraft is still.
  • q is what the wing actually feels: lift, drag and loads scale with it.

los.lo: State the formula for ‘dynamic pressure’.
los.title: Formula for dynamic pressure
los.html:
Theory & physics

q = ½ ρ V², with ρ the air density and V the true airspeed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • q grows with the square of speed: double the TAS → four times q.
  • Use TAS and actual density, or EAS and sea-level density: both give the same q.

los.lo: Describe dynamic pressure in terms of an indication of the energy in the system, and how it is related to indicated airspeed (IAS) and air density for a given altitude and speed.
los.title: Dynamic pressure and IAS
los.html:
Theory & physics

Dynamic pressure is the energy of the airflow, and it is what the airspeed indicator measures: same IAS = same q = same aerodynamic forces at the same angle of attack, at any altitude. Because ρ falls with height, a higher TAS is needed to give the same q at altitude.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Stall speed, VA, flap and gear limits stay roughly constant as IAS, not TAS.
  • Same IAS at higher altitude → higher TAS.

los.lo: State Bernoulli’s equation for incompressible flow.
los.title: Bernoulli's equation
los.html:
Theory & physics

For steady, incompressible flow without friction, along a streamline: p + ½ ρ V² = constant (the total pressure). Where the air speeds up its static pressure falls; where it slows its static pressure rises.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Energy is traded between pressure and speed; the total stays the same.
  • Valid only for incompressible (low-speed) flow without friction.

los.lo: Define ‘total pressure’ and explain that the total pressure differs in different systems.
los.title: Total pressure
los.html:
Theory & physics

Total pressure = static + dynamic pressure: the pressure where the flow is brought fully to rest, as in a pitot tube. It is constant only within one flow system: it rises where energy is added (propeller disc, compressor) and falls where energy is lost (boundary layer, wake, shock wave).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Total pressure behind a propeller is higher than in the free stream.
  • Across a shock wave total pressure is lost.

los.lo: Apply Bernoulli’s equation to flow through a venturi stream tube for incompressible flow.
los.title: Bernoulli in a venturi
los.html:
Theory & physics

Combining continuity and Bernoulli in a venturi: at the throat the area is smallest, so speed is highest and static pressure lowest; downstream both return to their entry values (ignoring friction). Total pressure stays the same throughout.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Throat: max speed, min static pressure, same total pressure.
  • A wing's curved upper surface acts like half a venturi, lowering the pressure above it.

los.lo: Describe how IAS is acquired from the pitot static system.
los.title: How IAS is obtained
los.html:
Theory & physics

The pitot tube senses total pressure, the static ports static pressure. The ASI measures the difference, pT − p = q, and is calibrated to show the speed that would give that q at ISA sea-level density.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The ASI measures dynamic pressure, then converts it to a speed using sea-level density.
  • Blocked pitot or static gives wrong IAS (covered in 022).

los.lo: Describe the relationship between density, temperature, and pressure for air.
los.title: The equation of state
los.html:
Theory & physics

Pressure, density and temperature are linked by the gas law p = ρ × R × T (T in kelvin, R = 287 J/kg/K). At constant pressure, ρ is inversely proportional to absolute temperature; at constant temperature, ρ is proportional to pressure.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Always convert to kelvin: going from 15 °C to 30 °C is 288 K → 303 K, only about 5 % less dense, not half.
  • Doubling pressure at constant T doubles density.

los.lo: Explain the equation of continuity and its application to the flow through a stream tube.
los.title: Equation of continuity
los.html:
Theory & physics

In steady flow the mass flow through every section of a stream tube is the same: ρ × A × V = constant. For incompressible flow this becomes A × V = constant: where the tube narrows the air speeds up, where it widens it slows down.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Area halves → speed doubles (incompressible).
  • At supersonic speed this reverses: a diverging duct speeds the flow up.

los.lo: Define ‘IAS’, ‘CAS’, ‘EAS’, and ‘TAS’.
los.title: IAS, CAS, EAS and TAS
los.html:
Theory & physics

IAS: the instrument reading. CAS: IAS corrected for instrument and position error. EAS: CAS corrected for compressibility; it fixes q exactly (q = ½ ρ₀ EAS²). TAS: the real speed through the air, EAS × √(ρ₀/ρ).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Order of corrections: I → C → E → T ("ICE-T").
  • At altitude TAS > EAS; at low speed and altitude CAS ≈ EAS.
  • Compressibility correction makes EAS less than CAS at high speed.

los.lo: Describe steady and unsteady airflow.
los.title: Steady and unsteady flow
los.html:
Theory & physics

Flow is steady when speed, pressure and direction at each fixed point stay constant over time; unsteady when they change, as in gusts, wakes or behind a stalled wing.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • In steady flow streamlines are also the particle paths.

los.lo: Explain the concept of a streamline and a stream tube.
los.title: Streamlines and stream tubes
los.html:
Theory & physics

A streamline is everywhere parallel to the local flow, so no air crosses it. A bundle of streamlines forms a stream tube, whose walls no air crosses either: it behaves like a pipe.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • No flow crosses a streamline or a stream-tube wall.
  • Closely spaced streamlines = fast flow, low static pressure.

los.lo: Describe and explain airflow through a stream tube.
los.title: Flow through a stream tube
los.html:
Theory & physics

Where streamlines converge the tube narrows, the air speeds up and its static pressure falls; where they diverge the air slows and the pressure rises (continuity plus Bernoulli).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Converging streamlines → higher speed, lower pressure.

los.lo: Explain the difference between two- and three-dimensional airflow.
los.title: 2-D and 3-D flow
los.html:
Theory & physics

Two-dimensional flow is around a section of infinite span, identical in every slice, with no spanwise flow: it describes an aerofoil. Three-dimensional flow is around a real finite wing, with flow round the tips, spanwise flow and tip vortices, which bring induced drag.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Induced drag exists only in 3-D flow.
  • Section (2-D) data give a steeper lift curve than the real wing.

los.lo: Describe the originating point and direction of the resultant force caused by the pressure distribution around an aerofoil.
los.title: Resultant aerodynamic force
los.html:
Theory & physics

The pressures and friction on an aerofoil add up to one resultant aerodynamic force, acting at the centre of pressure (CP) on the chord line, pointing upwards and inclined backwards.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The CP moves with angle of attack, which is why the aerodynamic centre is used instead.

los.lo: Resolve the resultant force into the components ‘lift’ and ‘drag’.
los.title: Lift and drag components
los.html:
Theory & physics

The resultant is resolved into lift, perpendicular to the relative airflow, and drag, parallel to it in the direction of the flow.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Components are taken relative to the relative airflow, not the chord or the horizon.

los.lo: Describe the direction of lift and drag.
los.title: Direction of lift and drag
los.html:
Theory & physics

Lift is at right angles to the flight path (relative airflow), so it is not necessarily vertical: it tilts in a climb, descent or turn. Drag always acts directly opposite the flight path through the air.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • In a climb, lift is less than weight; it is not vertical.
  • In a bank, lift tilts with the wings.

los.lo: Define the ‘aerodynamic moment’.
los.title: Aerodynamic moment
los.html:
Theory & physics

Lift and drag are placed at the aerodynamic centre (AC), about 25 % chord in subsonic flow, plus a pitching moment that does not change with angle of attack. This is the aerodynamic moment of the force about the AC.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • AC is fixed (≈ 25 % chord); CP moves.
  • About the AC, the moment is constant with α.

los.lo: List the factors that affect the aerodynamic moment.
los.title: Factors affecting the aerodynamic moment
los.html:
Theory & physics

M = CM × q × S × c: it depends on the section's camber (through CM), the dynamic pressure, the wing area and the chord.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Moment grows with q, so with IAS squared.
  • Angle of attack is not a factor (about the AC).

los.lo: Describe the aerodynamic moment for a symmetrical aerofoil.
los.title: Moment of a symmetrical aerofoil
los.html:
Theory & physics

On a symmetrical aerofoil the CP stays at the AC, so the pitching moment about the AC is zero.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Symmetrical section: CP fixed at about 25 % chord, CM,AC = 0.

los.lo: Describe the aerodynamic moment for a positively and negatively cambered aerofoil.
los.title: Moment of a cambered aerofoil
los.html:
Theory & physics

A positively cambered aerofoil has a nose-down moment about the AC, constant with angle of attack. A negatively cambered one has a nose-up moment.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Positive camber → nose-down CM,AC.
  • On a cambered section the CP moves forward as α increases.

los.lo: Define ‘angle of attack’ (alpha).
los.title: Angle of attack
los.html:
Theory & physics

The angle of attack (α) is the angle between the chord line and the relative airflow.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Not the same as pitch attitude or angle of incidence.
  • The wing stalls at a critical angle of attack, at any speed.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of an aerofoil section: leading edge.
los.title: Leading edge
los.html:
Theory & physics

The leading edge is the front of the aerofoil section, the first part to meet the airflow.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The leading edge is one end of the chord line.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of an aerofoil section: trailing edge.
los.title: Trailing edge
los.html:
Theory & physics

The trailing edge is the sharp rear edge where the upper and lower surface flows meet.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The trailing edge is the other end of the chord line.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of an aerofoil section: chord line.
los.title: Chord line
los.html:
Theory & physics

The chord line is the straight line from the leading edge to the trailing edge; its length is the chord.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Angle of attack and incidence are both measured from the chord line, not the camber line.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of an aerofoil section: thickness-to-chord ratio or relative thickness.
los.title: Thickness-to-chord ratio
los.html:
Theory & physics

The thickness-to-chord ratio (relative thickness) is maximum thickness ÷ chord, as a percentage: around 12 % for a subsonic wing, less for high-speed wings.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Thinner sections → higher critical Mach number.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of an aerofoil section: location of maximum thickness.
los.title: Location of maximum thickness
los.html:
Theory & physics

The position of maximum thickness is given as a percentage of chord from the leading edge. Further aft favours laminar flow and a higher critical Mach number.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Measured from the leading edge, as % of chord.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of an aerofoil section: camber line.
los.title: Camber line
los.html:
Theory & physics

The camber line (mean line) runs midway between the upper and lower surfaces, from leading edge to trailing edge.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Symmetrical section: camber line = chord line.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of an aerofoil section: camber.
los.title: Camber
los.html:
Theory & physics

Camber is the greatest distance between the camber line and the chord line, expressed as a percentage of chord.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • More camber → more lift at a given α and a lower stall speed (that's what flaps add).

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of an aerofoil section: nose radius.
los.title: Nose radius
los.html:
Theory & physics

The nose radius (leading-edge radius) describes how blunt the leading edge is. A large radius suits low speed and high lift; a sharp one suits high speed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Sharp leading edge → stalls at a lower α, more abruptly.

los.lo: Describe a symmetrical and an asymmetrical aerofoil section.
los.title: Symmetrical and asymmetrical sections
los.html:
Theory & physics

A symmetrical section has no camber: camber line = chord line, and it gives no lift at zero α. An asymmetrical (cambered) section has a curved camber line and gives lift at zero α.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Cambered section: zero-lift angle is negative.
  • Symmetrical section: zero-lift angle = 0°.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of a wing: span.
los.title: Span
los.html:
Theory & physics

The span (b) is the distance from wing tip to wing tip.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Span appears squared in aspect ratio: A = b²/S.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of a wing: tip and root chord.
los.title: Root and tip chord
los.html:
Theory & physics

The root chord is the chord at the aircraft centreline; the tip chord is the chord at the wing tip.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Root chord is at the centreline, not at the fuselage side.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of a wing: taper ratio.
los.title: Taper ratio
los.html:
Theory & physics

Taper ratio = tip chord ÷ root chord: 1 for a rectangular wing, 0 for a pointed delta.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Taper ratio is tip over root, so it is always ≤ 1 for a normal wing.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of a wing: wing area.
los.title: Wing area
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wing area (S) is the planform area projected onto a flat surface, normally including the part inside the fuselage.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The section covered by the fuselage counts in S.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of a wing: wing planform.
los.title: Wing planform
los.html:
Theory & physics

The planform is the wing's shape seen from above: rectangular, tapered, elliptical, swept or delta. It affects induced drag and where the stall starts.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Elliptical planform → minimum induced drag for a given aspect ratio.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of a wing: mean geometric chord.
los.title: Mean geometric chord
los.html:
Theory & physics

The mean geometric chord = wing area ÷ span, S / b.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • MGC is pure geometry; the MAC is the aerodynamic equivalent.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of a wing: mean aerodynamic chord (MAC).
los.title: Mean aerodynamic chord
los.html:
Theory & physics

The MAC is the chord of an imaginary rectangular wing with the same aerodynamic forces and moments as the real one. CG position and limits are quoted as % MAC.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • CG at "25 % MAC" means a quarter of the MAC length behind its leading edge.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of a wing: aspect ratio.
los.title: Aspect ratio
los.html:
Theory & physics

Aspect ratio = span ÷ mean chord = b² / S. Glider ≈ 25, airliner ≈ 9.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • High aspect ratio → less induced drag and a steeper lift curve.
  • Example: b = 34 m, S = 122 m² → A ≈ 9.5.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of a wing: dihedral angle.
los.title: Dihedral angle
los.html:
Theory & physics

Dihedral is the upward angle of the wing from root to tip, seen from the front; a downward angle is anhedral.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Dihedral increases lateral (roll) stability.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of a wing: sweep angle.
los.title: Sweep angle
los.html:
Theory & physics

Sweep angle is the angle between a spanwise line, usually the quarter-chord line, and the lateral axis.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Sweep raises the critical Mach number.
  • Measured at the 25 % chord line by convention.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of a wing: wing twist, geometric and aerodynamic.
los.title: Wing twist
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wing twist varies α along the span. Geometric twist (washout) reduces the angle of incidence from root to tip; aerodynamic twist does the same by changing the section towards the tip (less camber, lower zero-lift angle). Both make the root stall before the tip.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Washout = lower incidence at the tip.
  • Purpose: keep aileron control at the stall.

los.lo: Describe the following parameter of a wing: angle of incidence. Remark: In certain textbooks, angle of incidence is used as angle of attack (alpha). For Part-FCL theoretical knowledge examination purposes, this use is discontinued, and the angle of incidence is defined as the angle between the aeroplane longitudinal axis and the wing-root chord line.
los.title: Angle of incidence
los.html:
Theory & physics

The angle of incidence is the angle between the aircraft's longitudinal axis and the wing-root chord line. It is fixed by design.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • For EASA, angle of incidence ≠ angle of attack.
  • It does not change in flight (unlike α).

los.lo: Describe the streamline pattern around an aerofoil.
los.title: Streamline pattern round an aerofoil
los.html:
Theory & physics

Parallel streamlines approach the wing, curve upwards ahead of the leading edge, divide at the stagnation point, pass over and under the section and leave the trailing edge deflected down. Above the curved upper surface they are squeezed together; below they stay further apart.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Close streamlines above = faster flow, lower pressure.

los.lo: Describe converging and diverging streamlines, and their effect on static pressure and velocity.
los.title: Converging and diverging streamlines
los.html:
Theory & physics

Where streamlines converge, the stream tube narrows: speed rises and static pressure falls. Where they diverge, speed falls and pressure rises.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Converging = faster + lower static pressure (continuity + Bernoulli).
  • Over the front of the upper surface they converge strongly; near the trailing edge they diverge.

los.lo: Describe upwash and downwash.
los.title: Upwash and downwash
los.html:
Theory & physics

Upwash is the upward deflection of the air ahead of the leading edge; downwash is the downward deflection behind the trailing edge. The net downward turning of the air is the reaction to lift.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Upwash ahead, downwash behind.
  • Downwash reduces the tailplane's angle of attack.

los.lo: Describe the stagnation point.
los.title: Stagnation point
los.html:
Theory & physics

The stagnation point is where the dividing streamline meets the leading edge. The air is brought to rest: speed zero, static pressure highest on the section, equal to total pressure (Cp = +1).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Highest pressure on the aerofoil is at the stagnation point, not on the lower surface.

los.lo: Describe the movement of the stagnation point as the alpha changes.
los.title: Stagnation point and angle of attack
los.html:
Theory & physics

As α increases, the stagnation point moves down and back along the lower surface of the leading edge, and the suction peak behind the leading edge sharpens. As α decreases it moves up towards the nose (onto the upper surface at negative α).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Increasing α → stagnation point moves down and aft.
  • This is what stall-warning vanes and tabs on the leading edge sense.

los.lo: Describe pressure distribution and local speeds around an aerofoil including effects of camber and alpha.
los.title: Pressure distribution
los.html:
Theory & physics

Air over the upper surface moves faster and has lower pressure (suction); under the lower surface at positive α it is slightly above ambient. About two-thirds of the lift comes from upper-surface suction, peaking just behind the leading edge. Increasing α strengthens the suction peak and moves it forward; camber spreads the suction along the chord and gives lift even at zero α.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Most lift comes from the upper surface.
  • Suction peak is near the leading edge, not at maximum thickness.

topics.title: Centre of pressure (CP) and aerodynamic centre (AC)

los.lo: Explain CP and AC.
los.title: CP and AC
los.html:
Theory & physics

The centre of pressure is where the resultant force acts; on a cambered section it moves forward as α increases (towards 25–30 % chord) until the stall, then jumps back. The aerodynamic centre is the fixed point (≈ 25 % chord, subsonic) about which the pitching moment stays constant. On a symmetrical section they coincide.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • CP moves, AC fixed.
  • Cambered: CP moves forward with increasing α.

los.lo: List two physical phenomena that cause drag.
los.title: Two causes of drag
los.html:
Theory & physics

Drag comes from friction in the boundary layer and from the pressure difference between the front and rear of the body (form drag).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Friction + pressure = profile drag of a section.

los.lo: Describe skin friction drag.
los.title: Skin friction drag
los.html:
Theory & physics

Skin friction drag comes from air viscosity: the boundary layer is slowed by the surface and drags the surface back. It depends on wetted area, surface roughness and whether the boundary layer is laminar or turbulent.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Turbulent boundary layer → much higher friction drag than laminar.
  • Dirt, ice and rivets increase it.

los.lo: Describe form (pressure) drag.
los.title: Form (pressure) drag
los.html:
Theory & physics

Form drag arises because pressure does not fully recover at the rear of a body: the boundary layer thickens or separates, leaving low pressure behind. Blunt bodies with separated flow have high form drag; streamlined bodies low.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Delaying separation reduces form drag (that's why a turbulent boundary layer can help a blunt body).

los.lo: Explain why drag and wake cause loss of energy (momentum).
los.title: Drag, wake and energy loss
los.html:
Theory & physics

Drag shows up as a wake of slowed, often turbulent air. That air has lost momentum; the force that removed it is the drag. The energy the engines supply to overcome drag ends up as motion and heat in the wake.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Drag = rate of momentum loss of the air.

los.lo: Explain the influence of alpha on lift.
los.title: Lift and angle of attack
los.html:
Theory & physics

As α increases, the air is turned more strongly, suction on top deepens and pressure underneath rises, so lift increases almost linearly, until the flow can no longer follow the upper surface: it separates and lift falls (the stall).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Lift rises with α only up to αCRIT.

topics.title: The lift coefficient (CL) - angle of attack (alpha) graph

los.lo: Describe the CL-alpha graph.
los.title: The CL–α graph
los.html:
Theory & physics

The lift curve plots CL against α. It is a straight line over most of its range, curving over near the top to a maximum, then falling.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The slope (dCL/dα) is about the same for symmetrical and cambered sections.

los.lo: Explain the significant points: point where the curve crosses the horizontal axis (zero lift); point where the curve crosses the vertical axis (alpha equals 0); point where the curve reaches its maximum (CLMAX).
los.title: Key points on the lift curve
los.html:
Theory & physics

Horizontal-axis crossing (CL = 0): the zero-lift α: 0° for a symmetrical section, negative (−2° to −4°) for a cambered one. Vertical-axis crossing (α = 0): zero CL for symmetrical, positive for cambered. Maximum: CLMAX at the critical α (≈ 15–20° clean).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Cambered wing: lift at α = 0, zero lift at a negative α.

los.lo: Explain why coefficients are used in general.
los.title: Why coefficients are used
los.html:
Theory & physics

A coefficient is a dimensionless number: force ÷ (dynamic pressure × area). It isolates the effect of shape and angle of attack, so a force can be worked out for any size, speed and density, and wind-tunnel results apply to the full-size aircraft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Coefficients have no units.

los.lo: Explain the lift formula, the factors that affect lift, and perform simple calculations.
los.title: The lift formula
los.html:
Theory & physics

L = CL × ½ ρ V² × S. Lift is proportional to density, TAS² (or EAS²), wing area and CL.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Double the speed at the same α → 4× lift.
  • Example: 0.5 × ½ × 1.225 × 60² × 30 ≈ 33 kN.
  • To keep L constant when speed falls, CL (α) must rise.

los.lo: Describe the effect of camber on the CL-alpha graph (symmetrical and positively/negatively cambered aerofoils).
los.title: Camber and the lift curve
los.html:
Theory & physics

Positive camber moves the lift curve up and to the left: lift at α = 0, a negative zero-lift α, usually a slightly higher CLMAX. Negative camber moves it down and right. The slope stays about the same.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Camber shifts the curve; it does not change its slope.

los.lo: Describe the typical difference in the CL-alpha graph for fast and slow aerofoil design.
los.title: Fast and slow aerofoils
los.html:
Theory & physics

A fast aerofoil (thin, little camber, sharp nose) has a lower CLMAX, stalls at a lower α, often abruptly. A slow aerofoil (thick, cambered, large nose radius) has a higher CLMAX at a higher stall α and a gentler stall.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Thin high-speed sections need high-lift devices for take-off and landing.

los.lo: Define ‘CLMAX’ (maximum lift coefficient) and ‘alphaCRIT’ (stalling alpha) on the graph.
los.title: CLMAX and αCRIT
los.html:
Theory & physics

CLMAX is the highest lift coefficient the wing can reach; αCRIT is the angle of attack at which it occurs. Beyond it CL falls: the wing has stalled.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The wing stalls at αCRIT at any speed or attitude.

los.lo: Describe CL and explain the variables that affect it in low subsonic flight.
los.title: What CL depends on
los.html:
Theory & physics

In low subsonic flight CL depends on angle of attack, section shape (camber, thickness, nose radius), planform and aspect ratio, configuration (flaps, slats) and surface condition (contamination, ice). Speed and density do not affect it directly; they are already in the formula.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Ice and contamination reduce CLMAX and the stall α.

los.lo: Describe the two-dimensional drag formula.
los.title: The drag formula
los.html:
Theory & physics

D = CD × ½ ρ V² × S. For a 2-D section CD is profile drag (friction + form); at a given CD, drag is proportional to dynamic pressure.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Same structure as the lift formula, with CD in place of CL.

los.lo: Discuss the effect of the shape of a body, cross-sectional area, and surface roughness on the drag coefficient.
los.title: Shape, area and roughness
los.html:
Theory & physics

CD depends strongly on shape: flat plate ≈ 1.2, sphere ≈ 0.5, streamlined body ≈ 0.05 (same frontal area). Larger cross-sectional area gives more drag at the same CD. A rough surface makes the boundary layer turbulent earlier and raises friction drag.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Streamlining cuts CD by a factor of ~20 compared with a flat plate.
  • Always check which reference area a CD uses.

los.lo: Define ‘angle of attack’ (alpha). Remark: For theoretical knowledge examination purposes, the angle-of-attack definition requires a reference line. This reference line for 3D has been chosen to be the longitudinal axis and for 2D the chord line.
los.title: Angle of attack of the aeroplane
los.html:
Theory & physics

For the whole aeroplane (3-D), the angle of attack is the angle between the longitudinal axis and the relative airflow. For a wing section (2-D) the reference is the chord line.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • 3-D reference: longitudinal axis; 2-D reference: chord line.

los.lo: Explain the difference between the alpha and the attitude of an aeroplane.
los.title: Angle of attack versus attitude
los.html:
Theory & physics

Attitude (pitch angle) is the angle between the longitudinal axis and the horizon; angle of attack is measured from the relative airflow. In level flight they are equal; in a climb attitude = α + climb angle; in a glide the nose can be below the horizon with positive α.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • A wing can stall at any attitude.
  • High nose attitude ≠ high angle of attack.

los.lo: Describe the general streamline pattern around the wing, tail section, and fuselage.
los.title: Streamlines round wing, tail and fuselage
los.html:
Theory & physics

Seen from above, the air does not flow straight back: under the wing it drifts outwards, over the wing inwards. Behind the wing it is deflected down (downwash), which changes the airflow reaching the tailplane.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The tailplane sits in the wing's downwash, at a reduced angle of attack.

los.lo: Explain and describe the causes of spanwise flow over top and bottom surfaces.
los.title: Causes of spanwise flow
los.html:
Theory & physics

Higher pressure under the wing pushes air outwards towards the tips; lower pressure on top draws air inwards towards the root. At the tips air flows round from below to the low-pressure upper side.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Lower surface: outboard; upper surface: inboard.

los.lo: Describe wing tip vortices and their contribution to downwash behind the wing.
los.title: Tip vortices and downwash
los.html:
Theory & physics

Upper and lower flows meet at the trailing edge at a small angle, forming a vortex sheet that rolls up into two wing-tip vortices. Seen from behind, the left one turns clockwise, the right anticlockwise: rising outboard, sinking inboard. They add to the downwash behind the wing.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Air rises outboard of the tips and sinks inboard.

los.lo: Explain why wing tip vortices vary with alpha.
los.title: Tip vortices and angle of attack
los.html:
Theory & physics

Vortex strength depends on the pressure difference between surfaces, so on CL. At high α (low speed, high weight, steep turns) vortices are strong; at high speed and low α they are weak.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Same lift, lower speed → higher CL → stronger vortices.

los.lo: Describe spanwise lift distribution including the effect of wing planform.
los.title: Spanwise lift distribution
los.html:
Theory & physics

Lift falls to zero at the tips. An elliptical distribution gives uniform downwash and the least induced drag for a given span. A rectangular wing has a fuller distribution towards the tips than ideal, but its root sections work at the highest local CL; a highly tapered or swept wing works its outboard sections hardest. The distribution also decides where the stall starts.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Elliptical = minimum induced drag.

los.lo: Describe the causes, distribution and duration of the wake turbulence behind an aeroplane.
los.title: Wake turbulence: distribution and duration
los.html:
Theory & physics

Vortices sink at about 300–500 ft/min, levelling off 500–900 ft below the flight path, and drift with the wind. Near the ground they spread sideways at about 5 kt; a 2–3 kt crosswind can hold the upwind vortex over the runway. They last up to 2–3 min, longest in calm, stable air.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Most dangerous: light crosswind and calm conditions.
  • Main hazard: induced roll beyond the follower's control authority.

los.lo: Describe the influence of flap deflection on the wing tip vortex.
los.title: Flaps and the tip vortex
los.html:
Theory & physics

Flaps concentrate lift on the inner wing. Vortices form partly at the outboard flap ends and the tip vortices start further inboard: the effective span shrinks and the wake is more concentrated. Flaps do not remove the wake.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Flap extension does not make wake turbulence go away.

los.lo: Describe the parameters that influence wake turbulence.
los.title: What drives wake turbulence
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wake strength depends on weight, speed, wingspan and configuration. Strongest from an aircraft that is heavy, clean and slow. Vortices start at rotation (nosewheel lift-off) and stop at nosewheel touchdown.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Worst case: heavy, clean, slow.
  • Land beyond the touchdown point and take off before the rotation point of a preceding heavy.

los.lo: Explain the factors that cause induced drag.
los.title: What causes induced drag
los.html:
Theory & physics

Induced drag is the price of making lift with a finite span: the pressure difference drives spanwise flow and tip vortices, which create downwash and tilt the lift backwards.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • No lift → no induced drag.

los.lo: Describe the approximate formula for the induced drag coefficient (including variables but excluding constants).
los.title: Induced drag coefficient formula
los.html:
Theory & physics

CDi = CL² / (π A e): proportional to CL², inversely proportional to aspect ratio A; e is the efficiency factor (1 ideal, ≈ 0.8 real).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Variables: CL² and A.

los.lo: Describe the relationship between induced drag and total drag in straight and level flight with variable speed.
los.title: Induced drag versus speed
los.html:
Theory & physics

In level flight L = W, so CL is high at low speed: induced drag is largest at low speed, falling roughly with 1/V². Parasite drag does the opposite. At low speed induced drag dominates the total.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Induced drag decreases as speed increases.

los.lo: Describe the effect of mass on induced drag at a given IAS.
los.title: Mass and induced drag
los.html:
Theory & physics

At a given IAS, more mass needs more CL; induced drag grows with weight². +10 % mass → about +21 % induced drag.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • +20 % mass → +44 % induced drag (1.2²).

los.lo: Describe the means to reduce induced drag: aspect ratio; winglets; tip tanks; wing twist; camber change.
los.title: Reducing induced drag
los.html:
Theory & physics

Higher aspect ratio; winglets (recover tip-vortex energy, increase effective span); tip tanks (act as end plates); washout; camber change along the span. All push the lift distribution towards elliptical or weaken the vortices.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Winglets increase effective aspect ratio without adding as much span.

los.lo: Describe the influence of lift distribution on induced drag.
los.title: Lift distribution and induced drag
los.html:
Theory & physics

The nearer the spanwise lift distribution is to elliptical, the lower the induced drag for a given lift and span.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • e = 1 only for an ideal elliptical distribution.

los.lo: Describe the influence of downwash on the effective airflow.
los.title: Downwash and the effective airflow
los.html:
Theory & physics

Downwash tilts the local airflow down, so the wing meets air at a smaller angle than the free stream.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Downwash reduces the effective angle of attack.

los.lo: Explain induced and effective local alpha.
los.title: Induced and effective angle of attack
los.html:
Theory & physics

Effective α = geometric α − induced α. The induced angle is the downward tilt of the local flow caused by downwash.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Geometric α must be larger to get the same lift on a finite wing.

los.lo: Explain the influence of the induced alpha on the direction of the lift vector.
los.title: Induced angle and the lift vector
los.html:
Theory & physics

Lift is perpendicular to the local (downwash-tilted) airflow, so it is tilted backwards by the induced angle. Its component along the flight path is induced drag.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Induced drag = rearward component of the tilted lift.

los.lo: Explain the relationship between induced drag and: speed; aspect ratio; wing planform; bank angle in a horizontal coordinated turn.
los.title: Speed, aspect ratio, planform and bank
los.html:
Theory & physics

Induced drag is inversely proportional to V² and to aspect ratio; least for an elliptical distribution; and in a level turn it grows with n² (n = 1/cos φ). At 60° bank (n = 2) it is four times larger.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • 60° bank → n = 2 → 4× induced drag.

los.lo: Explain the induced drag coefficient and its relationship with the lift coefficient and aspect ratio.
los.title: CDi, CL and aspect ratio
los.html:
Theory & physics

CDi rises with the square of CL and falls with aspect ratio. Example: A = 9, e = 0.8, CL = 0.5 → CDi ≈ 0.011; double CL → four times CDi.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Double CL → 4× CDi.

los.lo: Explain the influence of induced drag on: the CL-alpha graph, and show the effect on the graph when comparing high- and low-aspect ratio wings; the CL-CD (aeroplane polar), and show the effect on the graph when comparing high- and low-aspect ratio wings; the parabolic aeroplane polar in a graph and as a formula [CD equals CPD plus kCL2], where CD equals coefficient of drag and CPD equals coefficient of parasite drag.
los.title: Induced drag on the graphs
los.html:
Theory & physics

Lift curve: a low-aspect-ratio wing has a less steep curve and reaches CLMAX at a higher α; high aspect ratio = steeper curve, lower stall α. Polar: CD = CDP + k CL², a parabola; higher aspect ratio gives smaller k and a polar that rises less steeply.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Low AR: flatter lift curve, higher stalling α.
  • k = 1/(πAe).

los.lo: Describe the CL-CD graph (polar).
los.title: The drag polar
los.html:
Theory & physics

The polar plots CL against CD for the whole aeroplane: close to a parabola, offset from zero by the parasite drag CDP.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Each point on the polar is one angle of attack.

los.lo: Indicate minimum drag on the graph.
los.title: Minimum drag on the polar
los.html:
Theory & physics

Minimum CD is where the curve is closest to the CL axis (at or near CL = 0). More important: the tangent from the origin touches the curve at (CL/CD)max: least drag for the weight carried, flown at VMD.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • (L/D)max = tangent from the origin, not the lowest CD.

los.lo: Explain why the CL-CD ratio is important as a measure of performance.
los.title: Why L/D matters
los.html:
Theory & physics

L/D = lift per newton of drag: aerodynamic efficiency. Its maximum fixes the best glide angle, the minimum thrust in level flight and, for a jet, best endurance. Airliner ≈ 17–20; glider > 50.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Glide ratio = L/D: at L/D 18, 1 NM of height → 18 NM of glide.

topics.title: Total drag in relation to parasite drag and induced drag

los.lo: State that total drag consists of parasite drag and induced drag.
los.title: Total drag
los.html:
Theory & physics

Total drag = parasite drag + induced drag. Parasite drag is all drag not caused by producing lift; induced drag is the drag of producing it.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Only two families: parasite and induced.

los.lo: Describe the types of drag that are included in parasite drag.
los.title: Types of parasite drag
los.html:
Theory & physics

Parasite drag = form (pressure) drag + interference drag + friction drag.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Induced drag is not part of parasite drag.

los.lo: Describe form (pressure) drag and the factors which affect its magnitude.
los.title: Form drag
los.html:
Theory & physics

Form drag comes from the pressure difference between front and back when the flow does not close smoothly behind a body. It depends on shape and frontal area, and rises sharply with separation. Streamlining and fairings reduce it.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Separated flow → large form drag.

los.lo: Describe interference drag and the factors which affect its magnitude.
los.title: Interference drag
los.html:
Theory & physics

Interference drag appears where parts meet (wing–fuselage, pylon–wing, tail–fin): the interacting boundary layers and pressure fields make the combined drag exceed the sum of the parts. It depends on the angle between surfaces and the shape of the joint; fillets and fairings reduce it.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Fix: fillets/fairings at the junction.

los.lo: Describe friction drag and the factors which affect its magnitude.
los.title: Friction drag
los.html:
Theory & physics

Friction drag is boundary-layer shear. It depends on wetted area, surface roughness (dirt, insects, rivets, paint, ice) and the share of laminar vs turbulent boundary layer: turbulent has several times the friction.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Laminar = low friction; turbulent = high friction.

los.lo: Describe the relationship between parasite drag and speed.
los.title: Parasite drag and speed
los.html:
Theory & physics

Parasite drag is proportional to dynamic pressure, so it grows with IAS² (EAS²). Double the speed → 4× parasite drag.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Parasite drag ∝ V²; induced drag ∝ 1/V².

los.lo: Explain the total drag-speed graph and the constituent drag components.
los.title: The drag–speed curve
los.html:
Theory & physics

In level flight at a given weight, parasite drag rises as V² and induced drag falls as 1/V². Their sum, total drag, is a U-shaped curve.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Low speed: induced dominates; high speed: parasite dominates.

los.lo: Indicate the speed for minimum drag.
los.title: Minimum drag speed
los.html:
Theory & physics

VMD is the bottom of the total drag curve: there parasite drag = induced drag, and the aircraft flies at (L/D)max.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • VMD = best L/D = best glide angle.
  • At VMD the two drags are equal, not minimum individually.

topics.title: Variables affecting the total drag-speed graph

los.lo: Describe the effect of aeroplane gross mass on the graph.
los.title: Gross mass and the drag curve
los.html:
Theory & physics

A heavier aircraft needs a higher CL at every speed, so more induced drag: the curve moves up and to the right. Minimum drag rises in proportion to W; VMD rises with √W.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • (L/D)max is unchanged by weight; only the speed for it changes.

los.lo: Describe the effect of pressure altitude on: drag-IAS graph; drag-TAS graph.
los.title: Altitude and the drag curve
los.html:
Theory & physics

Against IAS/EAS the drag curve does not change with altitude (drag depends on q, which EAS fixes). Against TAS it moves to the right. So VMD is constant as an IAS but increases as a TAS.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Higher altitude: same IAS VMD, higher TAS VMD.

los.lo: Describe speed stability from the graph.
los.title: Speed stability from the drag curve
los.html:
Theory & physics

At constant thrust, the slope of the drag curve tells you whether a speed disturbance corrects itself (drag rises with speed) or grows (drag falls with speed).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Positive slope (above VMD) = stable.

los.lo: Describe non-stable, neutral, and stable IAS regions.
los.title: Stable, neutral and unstable regions
los.html:
Theory & physics

Above VMD: speed loss reduces drag, surplus thrust restores speed: stable. At VMD: drag barely changes: neutral. Below VMD (back side, reversed command): speed loss increases drag, speed keeps falling: unstable.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Back side of the drag curve = region of reversed command.

los.lo: Explain what happens to the IAS and drag in the non-stable region if speed suddenly decreases and why this could occur.
los.title: Speed loss in the unstable region
los.html:
Theory & physics

Below VMD, a sudden speed loss (gust, or raising the nose to correct a low glide path) increases drag; with thrust unchanged the aircraft keeps decelerating towards the stall. Typical on slow, heavy approaches or long slow climbs.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Correct with thrust, not just pitch.
  • Reason approach speeds are kept above VMD or flown with autothrust.

los.lo: Explain the influence of ground effect on wing tip vortices, downwash, airflow pattern, lift, and drag.
los.title: Ground effect on the airflow
los.html:
Theory & physics

Within about one span of the ground (strongly within half a span) the ground blocks the downwash and the tip vortices: vortices weaken, downwash is reduced, lift rises and induced drag falls.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Effect becomes significant below ½ span height.

los.lo: Describe the influence of ground effect on induced alpha and the coefficient of induced drag (CDi).
los.title: Ground effect: induced α and CDi
los.html:
Theory & physics

Less downwash → smaller induced α → lift tilted back less → CDi falls. At one-tenth span height CDi can be roughly halved.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Ground effect reduces induced drag, not parasite drag.

los.lo: Explain the effects of entering and leaving ground effect.
los.title: Entering and leaving ground effect
los.html:
Theory & physics

Entering: less induced drag (the aircraft floats), more lift, reduced tail downwash → nose-down tendency, possible change in static-port pressure and IAS. Leaving: induced drag rises, more α needed, nose-up tendency; lifting off too slow may cause sinking back.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Entering = float + nose-down; leaving = more drag + nose-up.

topics.title: Effect on stalling angle of attack (alphaCRIT)

los.lo: Describe the influence of ground effect on alphaCRIT.
los.title: Ground effect and αCRIT
los.html:
Theory & physics

Because effective α is higher, the wing reaches its critical angle at a lower geometric α: αCRIT is reduced in ground effect.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Stall occurs at a lower pitch attitude near the ground.

los.lo: Describe the influence of ground effect on the effective alpha and CL.
los.title: Ground effect: effective α and CL
los.html:
Theory & physics

At the same geometric α the effective α is higher, so CL is higher: the lift curve becomes steeper.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Same attitude → more lift in ground effect.

topics.title: Effect on take-off and landing characteristics of an aeroplane

los.lo: Describe the influence of ground effect on take-off and landing characteristics and performance of an aeroplane.
los.title: Ground effect in take-off and landing
los.html:
Theory & physics

Ground effect lets an aircraft lift off below the speed it can sustain in free air, risking a premature lift-off and sink. On landing it lengthens the float, especially with excess approach speed, increasing landing distance.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Excess speed + ground effect = long float.

los.lo: Describe the difference in take-off and landing characteristics of high- and low-wing aeroplanes.
los.title: High-wing versus low-wing
los.html:
Theory & physics

A low-wing aircraft's wing is closer to the ground, so it feels ground effect more than a high-wing: more float on landing and larger take-off changes.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Low wing = stronger ground effect.

subs.title: The relationship between lift coefficient and speed in steady, straight, and level flight

los.lo: Explain the effect on CL during speed increase/decrease in steady, straight, and level flight, and perform simple calculations.
los.title: CL and speed in level flight
los.html:
Theory & physics

In level flight L = W, so CL × V² = constant at a given weight and altitude. Faster → lower CL (lower α); slower → higher CL. Example: CL 0.4 at 200 kt → at 140 kt CL = 0.4 × (200/140)² ≈ 0.82.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • New CL = old CL × (old V / new V)².
  • Stall speed = V × √(CL / CLMAX).

los.lo: Explain, by using a graph, the effect on speed of CL changes at a given weight.
los.title: Speed for a given CL
los.html:
Theory & physics

CL against speed is a curve falling steeply at low speed and flattening at high speed (CL ∝ 1/V²). Any change in CL at a given weight means a change in speed; the minimum level-flight speed is where CL = CLMAX: the stall speed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Each α corresponds to one IAS at a given weight.

topics.title: Trailing-edge flaps and the reasons for their use in take-off and landing

los.lo: From the given relevant diagrams, describe or identify the following types of trailing-edge flaps: split flaps; plain flaps; slotted flaps; Fowler flaps.
los.title: Types of trailing-edge flap
los.html:
Theory & physics

Plain: rear of the wing hinges down; smallest CLMAX gain. Split: only a lower-surface plate hinges down; a bit more lift, lots of drag. Slotted: leaves a gap so high-energy air from below re-energises the flap's upper surface. Fowler: slides back (more area and chord) then down, usually slotted; largest CLMAX gain.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Largest gain: Fowler (camber + area).
  • Split flap: upper surface unchanged.

los.lo: Describe how the wing’s effective camber increases the CL and CD, and the reasons why this can be beneficial.
los.title: Effective camber, CL and CD
los.html:
Theory & physics

Flaps increase effective camber (and area for Fowler), giving more CL at every α and a higher CLMAX, so the aircraft can fly slower. They also add drag, which steepens the approach. Small settings: much lift, little drag (take-off). Large settings: much drag, little extra lift (landing).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Take-off flap = lift; landing flap = lift and drag.

los.lo: Describe their effect on: the location of CP; pitching moments (due to wing CP movement); stall speed.
los.title: Flaps: CP, pitch and stall speed
los.html:
Theory & physics

Flaps move the CP aft (extra lift over the rear of the wing) → nose-down pitching moment from the wing; changed downwash on the tail may reduce or reverse it depending on type. Higher CLMAX reduces the stall speed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Wing alone: flaps → CP aft → nose-down.

los.lo: Compare their influence on the CL-alpha graph: indicate the variation in CL at any given alpha; indicate their effect on CLMAX; indicate their effect on critical alpha; indicate their effect on the alpha at a given CL.
los.title: Trailing-edge flaps on the lift curve
los.html:
Theory & physics

Curve moves up and left: higher CL at any α; higher CLMAX; slightly lower αCRIT; a given CL at a lower α.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trailing-edge flaps reduce αCRIT.

los.lo: Compare their influence on the CL-CD graph: indicate how the (CL/CD)MAX differs from that of a clean wing.
los.title: Trailing-edge flaps on the polar
los.html:
Theory & physics

The polar moves to higher CL and higher CD; (L/D)max is lower than for the clean wing.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Flaps always reduce the best L/D.

los.lo: Explain the influence of trailing-edge flap deflection on the glide angle.
los.title: Flaps and the glide angle
los.html:
Theory & physics

Glide angle is set by L/D. Flaps lower L/D, so the glide is steeper: you can descend steeply without gaining speed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • More flap → steeper glide, not longer.

los.lo: Describe flap asymmetry: explain the effect on aeroplane controllability.
los.title: Flap asymmetry
los.html:
Theory & physics

One flap extended more than the other gives a strong roll towards the side with less flap, plus yaw, possibly beyond aileron authority at low speed. Systems compare both sides and stop the flaps on disagreement.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Roll is towards the wing with less flap (less lift).

los.lo: Describe trailing-edge flap effect on take-off and landing: explain the advantages of lower-nose attitudes; explain why take-off and landing speeds/distances are reduced.
los.title: Trailing-edge flaps in take-off and landing
los.html:
Theory & physics

Lower stall speed → lower take-off and landing speeds and shorter distances. The required CL comes at a lower α, so the nose attitude is lower: better view on approach, less tail-strike risk.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Flaps: lower speeds and lower nose.

los.lo: Explain the effects of flap-setting errors, such as mis-selection and premature/late extension or retraction of flaps, on: take-off and landing distance and speeds; climb and descent performance; stall buffet margins.
los.title: Flap-setting errors
los.html:
Theory & physics

Less flap than planned: real stall and VR higher than planned: longer run, may not lift off at VR, smaller stall margin at V2. More flap: shorter run but poorer climb gradient. Early or slow retraction: CLMAX drops while slow → sink or stall buffet. Late extension: fast and high; extension above VFE: structural damage.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Retract only at or above the minimum flap-retraction speeds.

topics.title: Leading-edge devices and the reasons for their use in take-off and landing

los.lo: From the given relevant diagrams, describe or identify the different types of leading-edge high-lift devices: Krueger flaps; variable camber flaps; slats.
los.title: Types of leading-edge device
los.html:
Theory & physics

Slats: small aerofoils that move forward and down, opening a slot (fixed, automatic or powered). Krueger flaps: hinge down and forward from the lower leading edge, adding camber and nose radius (often inboard on swept wings). Variable-camber flaps: leading-edge sections that curve down.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Krueger = from the lower surface of the leading edge.

los.lo: Describe the function of the slot.
los.title: Function of the slot
los.html:
Theory & physics

The slot feeds high-energy air from under the wing through an accelerating gap onto the upper surface. This energises the boundary layer and smooths the suction peak, so flow stays attached to a much higher α.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Slot = boundary-layer energiser, not a camber device.

los.lo: Describe how the wing’s effective camber increases with a leading-edge flap.
los.title: Leading-edge flaps and camber
los.html:
Theory & physics

Krueger and variable-camber flaps increase the effective camber at the front of the wing and its nose radius, letting air turn round the leading edge at high α without separating.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Bigger effective nose radius → later leading-edge separation.

los.lo: Explain the effect of leading-edge flaps on the stall speed, also in comparison with trailing-edge flaps.
los.title: Leading-edge devices and stall speed
los.html:
Theory & physics

They lower the stall speed by raising αCRIT, not by adding lift at a given α. Combined with trailing-edge flaps they give the largest reduction.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • TE flaps: more CL at same α. LE devices: higher αCRIT.

los.lo: Compare their influence on the CL-alpha graph, compared with trailing-edge flaps and a clean wing: indicate the effect of leading-edge devices on CLMAX; explain how the CL curve differs from that of a clean wing; indicate the effect of leading-edge devices on alphaCRIT.
los.title: Leading-edge devices on the lift curve
los.html:
Theory & physics

Slats extend the straight part of the curve to a higher CLMAX at a higher αCRIT; at normal α the curve is nearly unchanged (slightly lower with a slat). TE flaps instead shift the whole curve up and lower αCRIT.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Slats: CLMAX up, αCRIT up.

los.lo: Compare their influence on the CL-CD graph.
los.title: Leading-edge devices on the polar
los.html:
Theory & physics

A little extra drag at low CL, but the polar extends to higher CL; near the clean wing's stall they can give less drag than the clean wing.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Slats out in cruise = small drag penalty.

los.lo: Describe slat asymmetry: describe the effect on aeroplane controllability.
los.title: Slat asymmetry
los.html:
Theory & physics

With slats on one side only, the slat-less wing stalls at a lower α and drops first: sharp roll and possible spin entry near the stall.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The wing without slats stalls first.

los.lo: Explain the reasons for using leading-edge high-lift devices on take-off and landing: explain the disadvantage of increased nose-up attitudes; explain why take-off and landing speeds/distances are reduced.
los.title: Leading-edge devices in take-off and landing
los.html:
Theory & physics

They cut speeds and distances via a higher CLMAX, but that CL comes at a high α, so the nose attitude is high: poorer view and tail closer to the runway. Hence they are combined with TE flaps.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Slats alone → nose-high approach.
  • TE flaps: αCRIT down, nose lower. Slats: αCRIT up, nose higher.

los.lo: Explain the purpose of vortex generators.
los.title: Purpose of vortex generators
los.html:
Theory & physics

Vortex generators delay boundary-layer separation, keeping flow attached at high α and over control surfaces.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • They prevent separation; they do not add lift directly.

los.lo: Describe the basic operating principle of vortex generators.
los.title: How vortex generators work
los.html:
Theory & physics

Small vanes set at an angle to the flow each shed a small, strong vortex that mixes fast outer air into the boundary layer, energising it to resist an adverse pressure gradient.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Mechanism: mixing energy into the boundary layer.

los.lo: State their advantages and disadvantages.
los.title: Vortex generators: pros and cons
los.html:
Theory & physics

Advantages: delay separation at high α, keep controls effective, reduce shock-induced separation at high speed. Disadvantages: small parasite drag penalty in cruise, weight, maintenance.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Cost: more drag in cruise.

subs.title: Means to reduce the CL-CD ratio

topics.title: Spoilers and the reasons for their use in the different phases of flight

los.lo: Describe the aerodynamic functioning of spoilers: roll spoilers; flight spoilers (speed brakes); ground spoilers (lift dumpers).
los.title: Types of spoiler
los.html:
Theory & physics

Spoilers hinge up from the upper surface ahead of the flaps, destroying lift behind them and adding drag. Roll spoilers rise on one wing with the aileron. Flight spoilers (speed brakes) rise symmetrically in flight. Ground spoilers (lift dumpers) rise fully after touchdown or in a rejected take-off, putting weight on the wheels.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Lift dumpers improve braking, not just drag.
  • Roll spoiler rises on the down-going wing.

los.lo: Describe the effect of spoilers on the CL-alpha graph and stall speed.
los.title: Spoilers on the lift curve
los.html:
Theory & physics

Spoilers move the curve down: lower CL at any α and lower CLMAX, so the stall speed rises.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Speed brakes near the stall are dangerous.

los.lo: Describe the influence of spoilers on the CL-CD graph and lift-drag ratio.
los.title: Spoilers on the polar
los.html:
Theory & physics

Less lift and more drag: the L/D ratio falls.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Spoilers = lower L/D, steeper descent.

topics.title: Speed brakes and the reasons for their use in the different phases of flight

los.lo: Describe speed brakes and the reasons for using them in the different phases of flight.
los.title: Speed brakes and their use
los.html:
Theory & physics

Speed brakes (wing spoiler panels, fuselage or tail-cone panels) add drag to descend steeply without gaining speed, slow down quickly (e.g. ATC speed restrictions) and manage energy on approach.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • They trade height or speed for drag, not lift.

los.lo: State their influence on the CL-CD graph and lift-drag ratio.
los.title: Speed brakes on the polar
los.html:
Theory & physics

The polar moves right (more CD at every CL), so (L/D)max is lower.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Lower L/D → steeper glide.

los.lo: Explain how speed brakes increase parasite drag.
los.title: How speed brakes add parasite drag
los.html:
Theory & physics

They add form drag and create separated flow behind them, raising parasite drag.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Speed brakes increase parasite, not induced, drag.

los.lo: Describe how speed brakes affect the minimum drag speed.
los.title: Speed brakes and VMD
los.html:
Theory & physics

Parasite drag rises while induced drag is unchanged, so they become equal at a lower speed: VMD decreases.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Speed brakes out → VMD down.

los.lo: Describe their effect on rate and angle of descent.
los.title: Speed brakes and descent
los.html:
Theory & physics

With extra drag the aircraft descends at a steeper angle and higher rate at the same speed, or at the same rate at a lower speed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Same speed, more drag → higher rate of descent.

los.lo: Describe the locations on an aeroplane where ice build-up will occur during flight.
los.title: Where ice builds up
los.html:
Theory & physics

Ice forms where air meets the surface head-on with small radii: leading edges of wing, tailplane and fin; engine intakes, propellers; probes, antennas, wipers; windscreen. Thin surfaces like the tailplane collect ice faster than thick wing roots.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Small radius = high collection efficiency = more ice.

los.lo: Explain the aerodynamic effects of ice and other contaminants on: lift (maximum CL); drag; stall speed; alphaCRIT; stability and controllability.
los.title: Aerodynamic effects of ice and contamination
los.html:
Theory & physics

Even sandpaper-rough frost can: cut CLMAX (≈ 30 % or more); increase drag; raise the stall speed (15–20 % or more); lower αCRIT, so the wing may stall before the stall warning; cause tailplane stall, heavy or snatching ailerons and instability.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Stall warning is set for a clean wing.

los.lo: Explain the aerodynamic effects of icing during take-off.
los.title: Icing during take-off
los.html:
Theory & physics

Take-off is the worst case: high α near the ground with no height to recover. Rotating at the normal speed with a contaminated wing can give a stall, wing drop or failure to climb out of ground effect. Hence the clean wing concept: no take-off with frost, ice or snow on critical surfaces.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Even frost on the wing = no take-off.

topics.title: Deformation and modification of airframe, ageing aeroplanes

los.lo: Describe the effect of airframe deformation and modification of an ageing aeroplane on aeroplane performance.
los.title: Ageing airframes and performance
los.html:
Theory & physics

Dents, distortion, poorly fitting panels, repairs, protruding fasteners, worn seals, mis-rigging and extra antennas add parasite drag and asymmetries needing constant trim: higher fuel burn, lower performance (covered by performance factors).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Effect: more drag, more fuel, permanent out-of-trim.

los.lo: Explain the effect on boundary layer condition of an ageing aeroplane.
los.title: Boundary layer on an ageing aircraft
los.html:
Theory & physics

Roughness and steps make the boundary layer turn turbulent earlier and thicken: more friction drag and earlier separation, especially on laminar-flow surfaces.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Earlier transition → more friction drag.

los.lo: Define ‘speed of sound’.
los.title: Speed of sound
los.html:
Theory & physics

The speed of sound is the speed at which a small pressure disturbance travels through the air.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • It is a property of the air, not of the aircraft.

los.lo: Explain the variation of the speed of sound with altitude.
los.title: Speed of sound and altitude
los.html:
Theory & physics

In ISA it falls with temperature as you climb: 661 kt at sea level, 573 kt at the tropopause (−56.5 °C, 36 089 ft), then constant above it.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Above the tropopause (ISA) the speed of sound stays constant.

los.lo: Explain the influence of temperature on the speed of sound.
los.title: Temperature and the speed of sound
los.html:
Theory & physics

a = √(γRT) or a ≈ 38.95 √T kt (T in kelvin). It depends only on temperature: warmer air → faster sound.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Pressure and density do not affect it on their own.
  • 15 °C → 288 K → ≈ 661 kt.

los.lo: Define ‘Mach number’ as a function of TAS and speed of sound.
los.title: Mach number
los.html:
Theory & physics

M = TAS / a (local speed of sound). M 0.8 = 80 % of the speed of sound in the surrounding air.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Uses TAS, not IAS.

topics.title: Influence of temperature and altitude on Mach number

los.lo: Explain the absence of change of Mach number with varying temperature at constant flight level and calibrated airspeed.
los.title: Mach at constant FL and CAS
los.html:
Theory & physics

At constant flight level and CAS, Mach number does not change with temperature: a warmer day raises the speed of sound, but lowers density, so TAS rises in the same proportion. Mach depends only on dynamic and static pressure.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Constant FL + CAS → constant Mach, whatever the temperature.

los.lo: Explain the relationship between Mach number, TAS and IAS during climb and descent at constant Mach number or IAS, and explain variation of lift coefficient, alpha, pitch and flight-path angle.
los.title: Mach, TAS and IAS in climb and descent
los.html:
Theory & physics

Climb at constant IAS: TAS rises, a falls → Mach rises. Climb at constant Mach: TAS falls (below the tropopause) and IAS falls faster, so CL and α rise; at a given vertical speed the flight-path angle increases, and pitch attitude rises. Reversed in descent.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Constant IAS climb → Mach increases.
  • Constant Mach climb → IAS decreases.

los.lo: Explain: risk of exceeding the maximum operation speed (VMO) when descending at constant Mach number; risk of exceeding the maximum operating Mach number (MMO) when climbing at constant IAS; risk of a low-speed stall at high altitude when climbing at a too low Mach number.
los.title: VMO, MMO and high-altitude stall risks
los.html:
Theory & physics

Descending at constant Mach, IAS rises → risk of exceeding VMO (hence the Mach→IAS crossover). Climbing at constant IAS, Mach rises → risk of exceeding MMO (hence the IAS→Mach crossover). Climbing at too low a Mach at high altitude → very low IAS, high CL → low-speed stall, made worse by compressibility.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Descent: watch VMO. Climb: watch MMO.

los.lo: State that compressibility means that density can change along a streamline, and that this occurs in the high subsonic (from Mach 0.4), transonic, and supersonic flow.
los.title: Compressibility
los.html:
Theory & physics

Compressibility means air density changes along a streamline. It becomes significant from about M 0.4 and applies through high subsonic, transonic and supersonic flow.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Below M 0.4 air is treated as incompressible.

los.lo: State that compressibility negatively affects the pressure gradient, leading to an overall reduction of the CL.
los.title: Compressibility and CL
los.html:
Theory & physics

Compressibility steepens the pressure gradients near the leading edge so the flow reaches separation sooner at high α: overall CL is reduced, and most clearly CLMAX falls.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • High Mach → lower CLMAX.

los.lo: State that Mach number is a measure of compressibility.
los.title: Mach number as a measure of compressibility
los.html:
Theory & physics

Mach number measures how significant compressibility is: the higher M, the larger the density changes.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Compressibility depends on Mach, not on IAS.

los.lo: Describe that compressibility increases low-speed stall speed and decreases alphaCRIT.
los.title: Compressibility, stall speed and αCRIT
los.html:
Theory & physics

Because CLMAX falls, the stall IAS rises and αCRIT falls at high Mach number.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Stall IAS at altitude is higher than at sea level.

los.lo: List the subdivision of aerodynamic flow: subsonic flow below compressibility; subsonic flow above compressibility; transonic flow; supersonic flow.
los.title: The four flow regimes
los.html:
Theory & physics

1. Subsonic below compressibility (≈ M < 0.4). 2. Subsonic above compressibility (M 0.4 to MCRIT). 3. Transonic (MCRIT to ≈ M 1.3). 4. Supersonic (above ≈ M 1.3).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Transonic starts at MCRIT, not at M 1.

los.lo: Describe the characteristics of the flow regimes listed above.
los.title: Characteristics of the flow regimes
los.html:
Theory & physics

Below compressibility: density constant, low-speed theory applies. Above compressibility: all subsonic but density changes matter; lift-curve slope rises with M. Transonic: mixed subsonic and supersonic flow with shock waves; lift, drag and moment change rapidly. Supersonic: supersonic almost everywhere, shocks at nose and leading edges.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Transonic = mixed flow.

los.lo: Explain why some transport aeroplanes cruise at Mach numbers above the critical Mach number (MCRIT).
los.title: Cruising above MCRIT
los.html:
Theory & physics

Many jets cruise slightly above MCRIT: a small weak shock costs little drag, while higher speed improves productivity and, with a supercritical wing, specific range. They stay below the sharp drag rise (MDD).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Above MCRIT but below MDD.

los.lo: Define a ‘shock wave’.
los.title: Shock wave
los.html:
Theory & physics

A shock wave is a very thin region where supersonic flow is slowed abruptly and pressure, temperature and density jump. It forms where supersonic flow must slow or turn and disturbances cannot travel ahead.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • A shock is always associated with supersonic flow ahead of it.

los.lo: Describe a normal shock wave with respect to changes in: static temperature; static and total pressure; velocity; local speed of sound; Mach number; density.
los.title: Changes across a normal shock
los.html:
Theory & physics

Across a normal shock: velocity ↓, Mach ↓ (to below 1), static pressure ↑, static temperature ↑, density ↑, local speed of sound ↑, total pressure ↓ (energy lost), total temperature unchanged.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Only velocity, Mach and total pressure fall.
  • Total temperature stays constant.

los.lo: Describe a normal shock wave with respect to orientation relative to the wing surface.
los.title: Orientation of a normal shock
los.html:
Theory & physics

On a wing, the normal shock stands roughly perpendicular to the surface, at the rear of the supersonic region above the wing.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Behind it the flow is subsonic.

los.lo: Explain the influence of increasing Mach number on a normal shock wave, at positive lift, with respect to: strength; position relative to the wing; second shock wave at the lower surface.
los.title: Mach number and the shock wave
los.html:
Theory & physics

As Mach rises at positive lift: the supersonic region grows and the shock gets stronger; it moves aft towards the trailing edge; a second shock forms on the lower surface (at a slightly higher M) and also moves aft, often reaching the trailing edge first.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Increasing M → shock stronger and further aft.

los.lo: Explain the influence of alpha on shock-wave intensity and shock-wave location at constant Mach number.
los.title: Angle of attack and the shock wave
los.html:
Theory & physics

At constant Mach, higher α speeds up the upper-surface flow: the upper shock becomes stronger and moves forward; the lower-surface shock weakens.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • More α → upper shock forward.

subs.title: Effects of exceeding the critical Mach number (MCRIT)

los.lo: Define ‘MCRIT’.
los.title: Critical Mach number
los.html:
Theory & physics

MCRIT is the free-stream Mach number at which the local flow somewhere on the aircraft first reaches Mach 1.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • At MCRIT the free stream is still subsonic.

los.lo: Explain how a change in alpha, aeroplane weight, manoeuvres, and centre-of-gravity (CG) position influences MCRIT.
los.title: What changes MCRIT
los.html:
Theory & physics

Anything accelerating the flow more over the wing lowers MCRIT: higher α, higher weight, manoeuvres (n > 1), forward CG (more tail down-load → more wing lift). An aft CG raises it slightly.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Heavier or pulling g → lower MCRIT.

los.lo: Describe the behaviour of CL versus Mach number at constant alpha.
los.title: CL versus Mach at constant α
los.html:
Theory & physics

At constant α, CL first rises with M above ≈ M 0.4 (stronger suction), then beyond MCRIT falls with shock-induced separation, and falls further supersonic.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Rise, then drop after MCRIT.

los.lo: Explain the consequences of exceeding MCRIT with respect to CL and CLMAX.
los.title: Exceeding MCRIT: CL and CLMAX
los.html:
Theory & physics

Above MCRIT, shock-induced separation occurs at lower α, so both CL at a given α and CLMAX are reduced.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • CLMAX falls above MCRIT.

los.lo: Explain the change in stall indicated airspeed (IAS) with altitude.
los.title: Stall IAS and altitude
los.html:
Theory & physics

A given IAS means a higher Mach at altitude; CLMAX falls with Mach, so the stall IAS rises with altitude (constant at low altitude). The margin between minimum and maximum speeds narrows (coffin corner).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • High altitude: stall IAS up, MMO IAS down.

los.lo: Discuss the effect on alphaCRIT.
los.title: Mach number and αCRIT
los.html:
Theory & physics
