Shock-induced separation makes αCRIT smaller at high Mach numbers.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • High Mach → stall at lower α.

los.lo: Explain the advantages of exceeding MCRIT in aeroplanes with supercritical aerofoils with respect to: speed versus drag ratio; specific range; optimum altitude.
los.title: Advantages of supercritical cruise
los.html:
Theory & physics

A supercritical aerofoil flies above MCRIT with a weak shock, giving a better speed/drag ratio, a better specific range (∝ TAS × L/D) and a higher optimum altitude.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Benefit comes from delaying the drag rise, not avoiding shocks.

los.lo: Describe wave drag.
los.title: Wave drag
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wave drag is the extra drag from shock waves: energy lost in the shock plus shock-induced boundary-layer separation behind it.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Two parts: shock loss + separation.

los.lo: Describe the behaviour of CD versus Mach number at constant alpha.
los.title: CD versus Mach at constant α
los.html:
Theory & physics

CD is nearly constant up to MCRIT, rises slowly, then very steeply from MDD, peaks near M 1, then falls in supersonic flow.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Drag peak is near M 1, not at MCRIT.

los.lo: Explain the effect of Mach number on the CL-CD graph.
los.title: Mach number and the polar
los.html:
Theory & physics

Above MCRIT, increasing Mach moves the polar to higher drag and a lower (L/D)max.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Higher Mach → lower best L/D.

los.lo: Describe the effects and hazards of exceeding MDRAG DIVERGENCE, namely: drag rise; instability; Mach tuck; shock stall.
los.title: Hazards beyond MDD
los.html:
Theory & physics

Beyond the drag divergence Mach number: steep drag rise; instability as shock positions change; Mach tuck (nose-down); shock stall (lift loss from shock-induced separation, with buffet).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Shock stall comes with high-speed buffet.

los.lo: State the relation between MCRIT and MDRAG DIVERGENCE.
los.title: MCRIT and MDD
los.html:
Theory & physics

MDD is always higher than MCRIT: shocks first appear at MCRIT, but drag rises sharply only once they are strong enough to cause separation (typically a few hundredths of Mach higher).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Order: MCRIT < MDD.

los.lo: Discuss the effect of Mach number on the CP location.
los.title: Mach number and CP position
los.html:
Theory & physics

Beyond MCRIT the shock moves aft and the low-pressure region behind it grows towards the trailing edge, so the CP moves aft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Above MCRIT: CP aft.

los.lo: Describe the overall change in pitching moment above MCRIT and explain the ‘tuck under’ or ‘Mach tuck’ effect.
los.title: Mach tuck
los.html:
Theory & physics

CP moves aft; on a swept wing separation starts near the roots (ahead of the CG) while the tips (behind it) keep lift; reduced downwash raises tail α. Result: a nose-down moment growing with Mach: Mach tuck. Uncorrected, it pitches down, speeds up and gets worse.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Mach tuck is nose-down and divergent.

los.lo: State the requirement for a Mach trim system to compensate for the effect of the CP movement and ‘tuck under’ effect.
los.title: Need for Mach trim
los.html:
Theory & physics

High-speed aircraft need a Mach trim system to compensate for the aft CP movement and tuck-under.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Purpose: keep a positive stick-force gradient with speed.

los.lo: Discuss the aerodynamic functioning of the Mach trim system.
los.title: How Mach trim works
los.html:
Theory & physics

It senses Mach number and trims the elevator or stabiliser nose-up automatically, in proportion to Mach above a threshold, so the pilot never has to push less to fly faster.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Mach trim moves the trim nose-up as Mach increases.

los.lo: Discuss the corrective measures if the Mach trim fails.
los.title: Mach trim failure
los.html:
Theory & physics

If Mach trim fails, the AFM imposes a lower maximum Mach number: slow down and stay below it so natural stability is sufficient.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Action: reduce speed to the reduced MMO.

los.lo: Discuss the effects on the effectiveness of control surfaces.
los.title: Controls at high Mach number
los.html:
Theory & physics

A shock ahead of a control surface separates the flow over it, and pressure changes from deflecting the surface cannot pass forward through the shock: reduced effectiveness, buzz, even hinge-moment reversal. Hence all-moving tailplanes and spoilers on fast aircraft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Control buzz = shock oscillating on the surface.

subs.title: Means to influence critical Mach number (MCRIT)

los.lo: Explain the influence of the angle of sweep on: MCRIT; effective thickness/chord change or velocity component perpendicular to the quarter chord line.
los.title: Sweep, MCRIT and effective thickness
los.html:
Theory & physics

A swept wing feels mainly the flow perpendicular to the quarter-chord line, V × cos Λ, so it behaves as if the Mach number were lower and looks thinner (longer chord along the flow): MCRIT rises. Example: M 0.85, 30° sweep → ≈ M 0.74 normal component.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Effective Mach = M × cos Λ.

los.lo: Describe the influence of the angle of sweepback at subsonic speed on: CLMAX; efficiency of and requirement for high-lift devices; pitch-up stall behaviour.
los.title: Sweepback at low speed
los.html:
Theory & physics

Lower CLMAX and flatter lift curve; high-lift devices less efficient but more needed; spanwise flow thickens the tip boundary layer so the tips stall first → loss of lift behind the CG → pitch-up, driving deeper into the stall.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Swept wing stall = tip first + pitch-up.

los.lo: Discuss the effect of wing sweepback on drag.
los.title: Sweepback and drag
los.html:
Theory & physics

Sweep reduces wave drag at high subsonic speed (higher MCRIT and MDD). At low speed it slightly increases induced drag (lower effective aspect ratio, poorer lift distribution).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • High speed: less wave drag. Low speed: slightly more induced drag.

los.lo: Explain the use of thin aerofoils with reduced camber.
los.title: Thin aerofoils with little camber
los.html:
Theory & physics

They accelerate the flow less, so local Mach stays lower and MCRIT is higher. Cost: lower CLMAX, sharper stall, less room for structure and fuel.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Thinner = higher MCRIT.

los.lo: Explain the main purpose of supercritical aerofoils.
los.title: Purpose of supercritical aerofoils
los.html:
Theory & physics

A flattened upper surface keeps the flow moderately supersonic over a long region ending in a weak shock well aft; much lift comes from aft camber (rear loading). Aim: delay and weaken the shock.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Recognise it: flat top, curved-up rear lower surface.

los.lo: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of supercritical aerofoils for wing design.
los.title: Supercritical aerofoils: pros and cons
los.html:
Theory & physics

Advantages: higher MDD for a given thickness, or a thicker wing for the same MDD (more fuel, lighter structure, less sweep or higher AR), less wave drag. Disadvantages: large nose-down pitching moment from rear loading, sensitivity to shape, complex manufacture.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Drawback: nose-down moment to trim.

los.lo: Explain the use of vortex generators as a means to avoid or restrict flow separation caused by the presence of a normal shock wave.
los.title: Vortex generators and shock-induced separation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Vortex generators ahead of the shock mix energetic air into the boundary layer, so it survives the pressure jump across the shock: less shock-induced separation, buffet and control buzz.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Placed ahead of the shock position.

chapters.title: Stall, Mach tuck, and upset prevention and recovery

los.lo: Define the ‘boundary layer’.
los.title: Boundary layer
los.html:
Theory & physics

The boundary layer is the thin layer next to the surface in which speed rises from zero at the surface to the outer flow speed. It is where friction acts.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • At the surface the air speed is zero (no-slip).

los.lo: Describe the thickness of a typical laminar and turbulent boundary layer.
los.title: Boundary-layer thickness
los.html:
Theory & physics

A laminar boundary layer is very thin (≈ 1 mm); a turbulent one is several times thicker, up to a few centimetres on a large wing.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Turbulent = thicker.

los.lo: Describe the properties, advantages and disadvantages of the laminar boundary layer.
los.title: Laminar boundary layer
los.html:
Theory & physics

Smooth layers sliding over each other. Advantage: low skin friction. Disadvantage: little energy near the surface, so it separates easily in an adverse pressure gradient.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Laminar: low drag, poor resistance to separation.

los.lo: Describe the properties, advantages and disadvantages of the turbulent boundary layer.
los.title: Turbulent boundary layer
los.html:
Theory & physics

Random mixing eddies. Disadvantage: higher skin friction, thicker. Advantage: mixing brings fast air to the surface, so it has more energy and resists separation much better.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Turbulent: more friction, better at staying attached.

los.lo: Define the ‘transition point’.
los.title: Transition point
los.html:
Theory & physics

The transition point is where the boundary layer changes from laminar to turbulent. It moves forward with higher speed, roughness and adverse pressure gradients.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Roughness or contamination → transition further forward.

los.lo: Explain why the laminar boundary layer separates easier than the turbulent boundary layer does.
los.title: Why laminar separates more easily
los.html:
Theory & physics

The slow-moving lower layers of a laminar boundary layer have too little momentum to keep going against rising pressure. In a turbulent layer, mixing keeps feeding momentum from the outer flow down to the surface.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Key word: momentum/energy near the wall.

los.lo: Describe why the airflow over the aft part of a wing slows down as the alpha increases.
los.title: Why rear-wing flow slows with α
los.html:
Theory & physics

Behind the suction peak, air must flow from low pressure back up to trailing-edge pressure: an adverse pressure gradient. Higher α → stronger suction peak → steeper pressure rise → the rear flow is slowed more.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Adverse gradient = pressure rising in the flow direction.

los.lo: Define the ‘separation point’ and describe its location as a function of alpha.
los.title: Separation point
los.html:
Theory & physics

The separation point is where the boundary layer stops and reverses. At small α it is at or near the trailing edge; as α increases it moves forward, with turbulent reversed flow behind it.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Increasing α → separation point moves forward.

los.lo: Define alphaCRIT.
los.title: Critical angle of attack
los.html:
Theory & physics

αCRIT is the angle of attack at which CL reaches its maximum. Beyond it separation spreads forward rapidly and lift falls: the stall.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The stall is defined by α, not speed.

los.lo: Describe in straight and level flight the influence of increasing the alpha and the phenomenon that may occur regarding: the forward stagnation point; the pressure distribution; the CP location (straight and swept-back wing); CL; CD and D (drag); the pitching moment (straight and swept-back wing); buffet onset; deterrent buffet for a clean wing at high Mach number; lack of pitch authority; uncommanded pitch down; uncommanded roll.
los.title: Approaching the stall: what changes
los.html:
Theory & physics

As α increases: stagnation point down and back; suction peak sharpens then collapses; CP of a straight wing moves forward then sharply back at the stall, but on a swept wing moves forward (tips stall first); CL peaks then falls; CD and drag rise steeply; pitching moment nose-down (straight wing) or nose-up (swept); buffet begins; at high Mach a deterrent buffet may be the limit; lack of pitch authority, uncommanded pitch-down or roll.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Straight wing: nose drops. Swept wing: pitch-up.

los.lo: Explain what causes the possible natural buffet on the aeroplane in a pre-stall condition.
los.title: Pre-stall buffet
los.html:
Theory & physics

The turbulent, separated wake hits the rear of the wing and the tailplane, shaking the structure and controls.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Buffet is a natural warning, caused by separated flow.

los.lo: Describe the effectiveness of the flight controls in a pre-stall condition.
los.title: Controls before the stall
los.html:
Theory & physics

Controls become less effective: ailerons work in disturbed, low-energy air and feel soft; the elevator may lose authority; controls may feel light.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Ailerons lose effectiveness first in a tip stall.

los.lo: Describe and explain the normal post-stall behaviour of a straight-wing aeroplane.
los.title: Post-stall behaviour of a straight wing
los.html:
Theory & physics

A well-designed straight wing stalls at the root first: lift lost ahead of the tail plus reduced downwash at the tail → nose-down pitch. If symmetrical, the nose drops and α falls by itself.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Straight wing: nose-down, self-recovering.

los.lo: Describe the effect and dangers of using the controls close to the stall.
los.title: Using controls near the stall
los.html:
Theory & physics

Pulling harder raises α further. Using aileron to lift a dropping wing increases that wing's α (down aileron = more camber), possibly stalling it fully → spin. Reduce α first; keep wings level with rudder where the type allows.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Don't pick up a dropping wing with aileron near the stall.

los.lo: Describe the deterrent buffet.
los.title: Deterrent buffet
los.html:
Theory & physics

Deterrent buffet is buffeting so strong it unmistakably discourages the pilot from increasing α further.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • It is stronger than normal buffet onset.

los.lo: Explain the occurrence of the deterrent buffet and why this phenomenon is considered to be a stall limit.
los.title: Deterrent buffet as a stall limit
los.html:
Theory & physics

In some aircraft, especially at high Mach, deterrent buffet appears before CLMAX and makes further α unacceptable, so it is treated as the stall limit and used to define the stall speed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Stall can be defined by buffet, not only by CLMAX.

los.lo: Explain VS0, VS1, VSR, and VS1G.
los.title: VS0, VS1, VSR and VS1G
los.html:
Theory & physics

VS0: stall/minimum steady speed in the landing configuration. VS1: in a specified configuration. VS1G: one-g stall speed at CLMAX. VSR: CS-25 reference stall speed (CAS, ≥ VS1G); take-off and landing speeds are multiples of it.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • "0" = landing configuration.

los.lo: Solve VS1G from the lift formula given varying CL.
los.title: VS1G from the lift formula
los.html:
Theory & physics

VS1G = √(2W / (ρ S CLMAX)): stall speed ∝ 1/√CLMAX. Example: 120 kt at CLMAX 1.5; with flaps 2.4 → 120 × √(1.5/2.4) ≈ 95 kt.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • New VS = old VS × √(old CLMAX / new CLMAX).

los.lo: Describe and explain the influence of the following parameters on stall speed: CG; thrust component; slipstream; wing loading; mass; wing contamination; angle of sweep; altitude (for compressibility effects, see 081 02 03 02).
los.title: What changes the stall speed
los.html:
Theory & physics

Forward CG → bigger tail down-load → higher VS (aft CG lower). Thrust component and slipstream with power → lower VS. Wing loading / mass → VS ∝ √(W/S). Contamination → lower CLMAX, higher VS. Sweep → lower CLMAX, higher VS. Altitude → stall IAS constant low down, rises at high altitude (compressibility).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Forward CG = higher stall speed.
  • Power on = lower stall speed.

los.lo: Define the ‘load factor n’.
los.title: Load factor
los.html:
Theory & physics

n = L / W, in g. Level flight: n = 1.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • n is lift relative to weight, not acceleration felt alone.

los.lo: Explain why the load factor increases in a turn.
los.title: Load factor in a turn
los.html:
Theory & physics

In a level turn, lift tilts by the bank angle φ; its vertical part must still equal weight, so n = 1 / cos φ. 60° bank → n = 2.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • 30° → 1.15; 45° → 1.41; 60° → 2.

los.lo: Explain why the load factor increases in a pull-up and decreases in a push-over manoeuvre.
los.title: Pull-up and push-over
los.html:
Theory & physics

Pull-up: lift must support weight and curve the path upwards → n > 1. Push-over: gravity supplies part of the curving force → n < 1, down to zero or negative.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Push-over can give zero or negative g.

los.lo: Describe and explain the influence of the ‘load factor n’ on stall speed.
los.title: Load factor and stall speed
los.html:
Theory & physics

VS(n) = VS1G × √n: stall speed rises with the square root of load factor.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • 2 g → stall speed × 1.41.

los.lo: Explain the expression ‘accelerated stall’. Remark: Sometimes, accelerated stall is also erroneously referred to as high-speed stall. This latter expression will not be used for Subject 081.
los.title: Accelerated stall
los.html:
Theory & physics

A stall at n > 1 (turn, pull-up) is an accelerated stall: it occurs above the 1-g stall speed and can be more abrupt. (Not called "high-speed stall" for 081.)

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Same αCRIT, higher speed.

los.lo: Calculate the change of stall speed as a function of the load factor.
los.title: Stall speed and load factor: calculation
los.html:
Theory & physics

VS = VS1G × √n. Example: VS1G 110 kt, n = 2.5 → 110 × 1.58 ≈ 174 kt.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Don't multiply by n; multiply by √n.

los.lo: Calculate the increase of stall speed in a horizontal coordinated turn as a function of bank angle.
los.title: Stall speed in a turn: calculation
los.html:
Theory & physics

VS = VS1G × √(1/cos φ). Example: 100 kt, 45° bank → 100 × √1.414 ≈ 119 kt. Factors: 30° × 1.07; 45° × 1.19; 60° × 1.41; 75° × 1.97.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • 60° bank → +41 % stall speed.

los.lo: Calculate the change of stall speed as a function of the gross mass.
los.title: Stall speed and mass: calculation
los.html:
Theory & physics

VS2 = VS1 × √(m2/m1). Example: 120 kt at 60 t → at 48 t: 120 × √0.8 ≈ 107 kt.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • 20 % lighter → about 10 % lower stall speed.

topics.title: The initial stall in spanwise direction

los.lo: Explain the initial stall sequence on the following planforms: elliptical; rectangular; moderate and high taper; sweepback or delta.
los.title: Stall pattern by planform
los.html:
Theory & physics

The stall should start at the root (ailerons keep working, buffet warns, nose drops). Elliptical: whole span at once, little warning. Rectangular: root first (most benign). Moderate taper: part-way out; high taper: near the tips. Swept/delta: tips first (spanwise flow) → pitch-up.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Rectangular = root first; swept = tip first.

los.lo: Explain the purpose of aerodynamic and geometric twist (washout).
los.title: Purpose of washout
los.html:
Theory & physics

Geometric twist lowers tip α; aerodynamic twist gives tips a section with a higher stall angle. Either way the root stalls first and ailerons stay effective into the stall.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Washout protects aileron control at the stall.

los.lo: Explain the influence of fences, vortilons, saw teeth, vortex generators, and strakes on engine nacelles.
los.title: Fences, vortilons, saw teeth, VGs, strakes
los.html:
Theory & physics

Fences: chordwise plates blocking outward boundary-layer flow. Vortilons: plates under the leading edge whose vortex acts as a fence at high α. Saw tooth (dog-tooth): leading-edge step creating a fence-like vortex. Vortex generators: re-energise the boundary layer. Nacelle strakes: shed a vortex over the wing at high α to restore flow disturbed by the nacelle/pylon.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Fences, vortilons and saw teeth all fight spanwise flow and tip stall.

los.lo: Explain why stall warning is necessary.
los.title: Why stall warning is needed
los.html:
Theory & physics

The stall must be avoided, and natural warning is not always enough: some wings give little buffet, and at high altitude or with contamination it may come late.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Natural buffet alone can't be relied on.

los.lo: Explain when aerodynamic and artificial stall warnings are used.
los.title: Aerodynamic or artificial warning
los.html:
Theory & physics

Aerodynamic (natural buffet) warning is accepted only if clear and early enough; otherwise artificial warning (horn, light, stick shaker) is required, and most airliners have it anyway.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Artificial warning when natural warning is insufficient.

los.lo: Explain why CS-23 and CS-25 require a margin to stall speed for take-off and landing speeds.
los.title: Certification speed margins
los.html:
Theory & physics

Operating speeds keep a margin above the stall for gusts, manoeuvres and errors: CS-25 VREF ≥ 1.23 VSR0, V2 ≥ 1.13 VSR; CS-23 approach ≥ 1.3 VS0. Stall warning must begin at least 5 kt (or 5 %) before the stall.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Memorise 1.23, 1.13, 1.3 and 5 kt / 5 %.

los.lo: Describe: buffet; stall strip; flapper switch (leading-edge stall-warning vane); angle-of-attack vane; angle-of-attack probe; stick shaker.
los.title: Stall-warning devices
los.html:
Theory & physics

Buffet: natural. Stall strip: wedge on the inner leading edge forcing root separation first. Flapper switch: leading-edge tab pushed up as the stagnation point moves down, triggering the horn. AoA vane: weathervane on the fuselage measuring α directly. AoA probe: pressure ports sensing α. Stick shaker: shakes the column near the stall.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Flapper switch is driven by stagnation-point movement.
  • Stall strip goes on the inboard leading edge.

los.lo: Describe the recovery after: stall warning; stall; stick-pusher actuation.
los.title: Recovery from warning, stall and pusher
los.html:
Theory & physics

Warning: reduce α until it stops, wings level, adjust thrust. Stall: push to reduce α first (even losing height), level wings, then thrust (carefully with underslung engines: nose-up moment), then recover the path avoiding a secondary stall. Stick pusher: don't fight it; then recover as from a stall.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • First action is always reduce α, not add power.

los.lo: Explain the difference between power-off and power-on stalls and recovery.
los.title: Power-on and power-off stalls
los.html:
Theory & physics

Power on: lower stall speed, higher nose; slipstream and torque make a wing drop and spin entry more likely, stall can be abrupt. Power off: higher stall speed, lower nose, usually gentler. Recovery: reduce α first, then power.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Power-on stall = wing drop risk.

los.lo: Describe stall and recovery in a climbing and descending turn.
los.title: Stalls in climbing and descending turns
los.html:
Theory & physics

Climbing turn: the outer wing has the higher α and stalls first → rolls outwards. Descending turn: the inner wing has the higher α → rolls inwards. Recover by reducing α first, then rolling level.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Climbing → outer; descending → inner.

los.lo: Describe the pitch-up effect on a swept wing aeroplane and also an aeroplane with a T-tail.
los.title: Pitch-up: swept wing and T-tail
los.html:
Theory & physics

Swept wing: tips (aft of CG) stall first, lift moves forward, nose pitches up, increasing α further. T-tail: at high α the tailplane enters the wake of the stalled wing and rear engines and loses effectiveness.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Pitch-up is self-aggravating.

los.lo: Describe super stall or deep stall.
los.title: Deep stall
los.html:
Theory & physics

Deep (super) stall: the aircraft settles at a very high α in a stable stalled state, the tailplane in the wing/engine wake and the elevator unable to lower the nose. Recovery may be impossible.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Typical of T-tail, rear-engine, swept aircraft.

los.lo: Describe the philosophy behind the stick-pusher system.
los.title: Stick-pusher philosophy
los.html:
Theory & physics

A stick pusher forcefully pushes the column forward at a set α so the aircraft never reaches the deep-stall region: prevent the stall rather than recover from it.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Pusher = prevention, not warning.

los.lo: Describe the factors that can lead to the absence of stall warning and explain the associated risks.
los.title: Absent stall warning
los.html:
Theory & physics

Warning may be absent or late with a contaminated wing (stalls at lower α than the system assumes), a failed or frozen AoA sensor, an unpowered or inhibited system, or at high Mach. Monitor speed and attitude; never accept contamination.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Contaminated wing: stall before the shaker.

los.lo: Describe the indications and explain the consequences of premature stabiliser stall due to ice contamination (negative tail stall).
los.title: Tailplane stall from ice
los.html:
Theory & physics

The tailplane normally makes a down-load at negative α. It ices faster than the wing; ice lets it stall at a smaller negative α: a negative tail stall. Signs: light or buffeting column, pitch oscillations, trim difficulty, then a sudden nose-down.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Tail stall = sudden nose-down, often right after flap extension.

los.lo: Describe when to expect in-flight icing.
los.title: When to expect in-flight icing
los.html:
Theory & physics

In visible moisture (cloud, rain, drizzle) from about 0 °C to −20 °C, in Cb down to −40 °C, and in freezing rain/drizzle below a warm layer. Most severe near 0 to −10 °C with large drops.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Need visible moisture + sub-zero airframe.

los.lo: Explain how the effect is changed when retracting/extending lift-augmentation devices.
los.title: Tail stall and flaps
los.html:
Theory & physics

Flap extension increases downwash, making tail α more negative, so tail stall is most likely just after flap extension (and with high power/speed). Recovery is opposite to a wing stall: retract flaps to the previous setting, pull back, reduce power if the procedure says so.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Tail stall recovery: flaps up, column back.

los.lo: Explain the effect of a contaminated wing on the stall speed and alphaCRIT.
los.title: Contaminated wing: stall speed and αCRIT
los.html:
Theory & physics

Contamination gives a higher stall speed and a lower αCRIT.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Both effects make the stall come sooner.

los.lo: Explain the hazards associated with airframe contamination when parked and during ground operations in winter conditions, and the aerodynamic effects when attempting a take-off.
los.title: Winter ground operations
los.html:
Theory & physics

Frost, snow and ice settle on parked aircraft; slush is thrown onto wings and gear during taxi. Taking off contaminated risks a stall at or just after rotation, wing drop, poor climb and more drag. Hence de-icing and anti-icing.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Any contamination on critical surfaces = no take-off.

los.lo: Explain de-icing/anti-icing holdover time and the likely hazards after it has expired.
los.title: Holdover time
los.html:
Theory & physics

Holdover time is the estimated time anti-icing fluid prevents frost and ice forming. It depends on fluid type and concentration, temperature, and precipitation type and intensity. After it expires the fluid may be saturated: a contamination check or re-treatment is needed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • HOT is an estimate; heavier precipitation shortens it.

los.lo: Describe the aerodynamic effects of heavy tropical rain on stall speed and drag, and the appropriate mitigation in such conditions.
los.title: Heavy tropical rain
los.html:
Theory & physics

A water film roughens the wing, thickens the boundary layer and adds mass: more drag, CLMAX down several per cent, higher stall speed. Avoid the heaviest cells, add speed margin, be ready for more thrust.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Heavy rain: drag up, stall speed up.

los.lo: Explain how to avoid spins.
los.title: Avoiding spins
los.html:
Theory & physics

A spin needs stall + yaw. Avoid it by not stalling and by staying coordinated (ball centred) near the stall.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • No stall, no spin.

los.lo: List the factors that cause a spin to develop.
los.title: What starts a spin
los.html:
Theory & physics

Stalling with sideslip/yaw, using aileron to pick up a wing near the stall, power asymmetry and propeller effects, and an aft CG.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Aileron near the stall can start a spin.

los.lo: Describe an ‘incipient’ and ‘developed’ spin, recognition and recovery.
los.title: Incipient and developed spin
los.html:
Theory & physics

Incipient: stall to about two turns, unsteady, quickest to recover. Developed: steady rotation, airspeed and descent rate. Standard recovery (unless the AFM says otherwise): power idle, ailerons neutral, full opposite rudder, elevator forward; when rotation stops: rudder neutral, wings level, recover from the dive.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Order: P-A-R-E (power, ailerons, rudder, elevator).
  • Airspeed in a developed spin is low and steady.

los.lo: Describe the differences in spin attitude with forward and aft CG.
los.title: CG and spin attitude
los.html:
Theory & physics

Forward CG: steeper, nose-down spin; easier recovery. Aft CG: flatter, faster rotation; recovery slow or impossible (less elevator and rudder effectiveness).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Aft CG → flat spin.

los.lo: Explain shock-induced separation, and describe its relationship with Mach buffet (high speed buffet) and Mach tuck.
los.title: Shock-induced separation, Mach buffet and Mach tuck
los.html:
Theory & physics

At high Mach the upper-surface shock becomes strong enough to separate the boundary layer behind it. The unsteady flow shakes the aircraft: Mach (high-speed) buffet. The same separation shifts the CP and changes the downwash: Mach tuck.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • One cause (shock-induced separation), two effects.

los.lo: Explain the concept of buffet margin, and describe the influence of the following parameters on the concept of buffet margin: alpha; Mach number; pressure altitude; mass; load factor; angle of bank; CG location.
los.title: Buffet margin
los.html:
Theory & physics

At altitude the aircraft is boxed between low-speed buffet (α too high) and high-speed buffet (Mach too high). The buffet margin is the extra load factor available before buffet. It is reduced by higher α, higher Mach, higher pressure altitude, higher mass, higher load factor/bank, and a forward CG.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Forward CG reduces buffet margin.

los.lo: Explain how the buffet onset boundary chart can be used to determine: manoeuvrability; buffet margin.
los.title: Using the buffet onset chart
los.html:
Theory & physics

For a given mass, CG and altitude, the chart gives the Mach numbers of low- and high-speed buffet at a given load factor. Use it to find available manoeuvre (n or bank) at the planned level, and the buffet margin.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Inputs: mass, CG, altitude (and Mach).

los.lo: Describe the consequences of exceeding MMO: light buffet, buffet onset.
los.title: Exceeding MMO
los.html:
Theory & physics

Beyond MMO the aircraft enters shock-induced separation: first light buffet, then stronger buffet onset, plus Mach tuck and an overspeed warning.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Overspeed → high-speed buffet.

los.lo: Explain ‘aerodynamic ceiling’ and ‘coffin corner’.
los.title: Aerodynamic ceiling and coffin corner
los.html:
Theory & physics

Climbing at a given mass, the low-speed buffet Mach rises and the high-speed buffet Mach falls. Where they meet at 1 g is the aerodynamic ceiling: only one Mach is possible. The region near it is the coffin corner.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • At the aerodynamic ceiling the margin is zero.

los.lo: Explain the concept of the ‘1.3g’ buffet margin altitude.
los.title: 1.3 g buffet margin altitude
los.html:
Theory & physics

Operators require 1.3 g before buffet onset in cruise (≈ a level turn at 40° bank or a strong gust). The 1.3 g altitude is the highest level giving that margin at the current mass.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • 1.3 g ≈ 40° bank.

los.lo: Find (using an example graph): buffet free range; aerodynamic ceiling at a given mass; load factor and bank angle at which buffet occurs at a given mass, Mach number, and pressure altitude.
los.title: Reading the buffet chart
los.html:
Theory & physics

Find: the buffet-free Mach range at a given mass, altitude and n; the aerodynamic ceiling (where the 1-g range shrinks to a point); the load factor and bank at which buffet begins at a given mass, Mach and altitude (bank = arccos(1/n)).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • n = 1.5 → bank ≈ 48°.

los.lo: Explain why descent increases the buffet free range.
los.title: Why descent widens the buffet range
los.html:
Theory & physics

Lower down, density is higher, so a given Mach gives a higher IAS and needs less CL, moving both boundaries away. Hence descending in severe turbulence or buffet at altitude.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Descend to gain buffet margin.

subs.title: Situations in which buffet or stall could occur

topics.title: Explain why buffet or stall occurs

los.lo: Explain why buffet or stall could occur in the following pilot-induced situations, and the methods to mitigate them: inappropriate take-off configuration, detailing the consequences of errors associated with leading-edge devices; steep turns; go-around using take-off/go-around (TOGA) setting (underslung engines).
los.title: Pilot-induced stalls
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wrong take-off configuration (slats/LE flaps not extended): αCRIT much lower, normal rotation can stall the wing after lift-off; mitigate with checks, config warnings and correct speeds. Steep turns: VS rises with √n; limit bank. TOGA go-around with underslung engines: strong nose-up moment, speed decays; control pitch firmly, trim, follow the procedure.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Underslung engines + thrust = pitch-up.

los.lo: Explain why buffet or stall could occur in the following environmental conditions at low altitude, and how to mitigate them: thunderstorms; wind shear and microburst; turbulence; wake turbulence; icing conditions.
los.title: Low-altitude weather stalls
los.html:
Theory & physics

Thunderstorms, wind shear, microbursts: sudden headwind loss or downdraft drops IAS and raises α; avoid, or fly the wind-shear escape (max thrust, pitch to shaker/guidance, no configuration change). Turbulence: gusts change α; fly turbulence speed. Wake turbulence: keep separation, stay above the leader's path. Icing: higher VS, lower αCRIT, tail stall; anti-ice, avoid, add margin.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Wind-shear escape: don't change configuration.

los.lo: Explain why buffet or stall could occur in the following environmental conditions at high altitude, and how to mitigate them: thunderstorms in the intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ); jet streams; clear-air turbulence.
los.title: High-altitude weather stalls
los.html:
Theory & physics

ITCZ thunderstorms: violent updrafts, embedded cells, ice crystals blocking pitots; avoid widely on radar. Jet streams: shear can change IAS by tens of knots toward either buffet boundary. CAT: no visual warning. Mitigate: fly a level with good buffet margin, use turbulence speed/Mach, descend if needed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Small margins up high: a gust can hit either boundary.

los.lo: Explain why buffet or stall could occur in the following situations, and how to mitigate them: inappropriate autopilot climb mode; loss of, or unreliable, airspeed indication.
los.title: Autopilot climb mode and unreliable airspeed
los.html:
Theory & physics

Vertical speed mode at high altitude holds the climb rate regardless of speed; as thrust available falls, speed decays toward the stall. Use a speed-on-pitch mode. Unreliable airspeed (blocked pitot/static, ice crystals): fly memorised pitch and thrust, follow the procedure.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • V/S mode at altitude can fly you into a stall.

topics.title: Recognition and explanation of stalled condition

los.lo: Explain why a stalled condition can occur at any airspeed, or attitude or altitude.
los.title: Stall at any speed, attitude or altitude
los.html:
Theory & physics

The wing stalls at αCRIT, so a stall can happen at any airspeed, attitude or altitude: steep turn at high speed, dive pull-out, nose-low descent.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • α, not speed, decides the stall.

los.lo: Explain that a stall may be recognised by continuous stall-warning activation accompanied by at least one of the following: buffet, that can be heavy; lack of pitch authority; uncommanded pitch down and uncommanded roll; inability to arrest the descent rate.
los.title: Recognising a stall
los.html:
Theory & physics

Continuous stall warning plus at least one of: buffet (possibly heavy), lack of pitch authority, uncommanded pitch-down or roll, inability to arrest the descent rate.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Warning alone = approach to stall; warning + one sign = stall.

los.lo: Explain that ‘stall warning’ means a natural or synthetic indication provided when approaching the stall that may include one or more of the following indications: aerodynamic buffeting; reduced roll stability and aileron effectiveness; visual or aural clues and warnings; reduced elevator (pitch) authority; inability to maintain altitude or arrest a rate of descent; stick-shaker activation.
los.title: What counts as stall warning
los.html:
Theory & physics

A natural or synthetic indication approaching the stall: buffeting, reduced roll stability and aileron effectiveness, visual or aural warnings, reduced pitch authority, inability to hold altitude or arrest descent, stick shaker.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Stall warning can be natural or synthetic.

los.lo: Define ‘static stability’: describe/identify a statically stable, neutral, and unstable condition (positive, neutral, and negative static stability), and explain why aeroplanes are statically stable.
los.title: Static stability
los.html:
Theory & physics

Static stability is the initial tendency, immediately after a disturbance, to return to equilibrium. Ball in a bowl = positive; on a table = neutral; on an upturned bowl = negative. Aircraft are made statically stable so they hold trim and recover from gusts without constant correction.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Static = initial tendency only, not the motion afterwards.

los.lo: Explain manoeuvrability.
los.title: Manoeuvrability
los.html:
Theory & physics

Manoeuvrability is the ease and speed with which the aircraft can be made to change attitude, flight path or load factor in response to the controls.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Measured by how readily it responds, e.g. stick force per g.

los.lo: Explain the relationship between static stability and manoeuvrability.
los.title: Stability versus manoeuvrability
los.html:
Theory & physics

They oppose each other: a very stable aircraft resists the pilot too, needing large forces and deflections; a less stable one is more manoeuvrable but harder to fly steadily. Airliners: moderate stability; fighters: little or none (computer-assisted).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • More stability = less manoeuvrability.

los.lo: Define ‘dynamic stability’: describe/identify a dynamically stable, neutral, and unstable motion (positive, neutral, and negative dynamic stability); describe/identify periodic and aperiodic motion.
los.title: Dynamic stability
los.html:
Theory & physics

Dynamic stability is the motion over time after a disturbance: dies away = positive; constant amplitude = neutral; grows = negative. Motion may be periodic (oscillating) or aperiodic (no oscillation). Static stability is necessary but not sufficient for dynamic stability.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Statically stable can still be dynamically unstable (growing overshoot).
  • Statically unstable is always dynamically unstable.

los.lo: Explain an equilibrium of forces and moments as the initial condition for static stability.
los.title: Equilibrium as the starting point
los.html:
Theory & physics

Stability is judged from equilibrium: the sum of all forces and all moments is zero, so the aircraft flies steadily without accelerating or rotating.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • No equilibrium → no meaningful stability assessment.

los.lo: Identify the forces considered in the equilibrium of forces.
los.title: Forces in equilibrium
los.html:
Theory & physics

Lift, weight, thrust and drag (plus any side force). In level flight lift = weight and thrust = drag.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Four forces (plus side force).

los.lo: Identify the moments about all three axes considered in the equilibrium of moments.
los.title: Moments about the three axes
los.html:
Theory & physics

About the CG: pitch about the lateral axis, roll about the longitudinal axis, yaw about the normal axis.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Pitch ↔ lateral; roll ↔ longitudinal; yaw ↔ normal.

los.lo: Discuss the effect of sum of moments not being zero.
los.title: Unbalanced moments
los.html:
Theory & physics

If the moments about an axis don't sum to zero, the aircraft rotates about it with an angular acceleration; trim, stabiliser or control deflection is needed to restore balance.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Net moment → angular acceleration, not constant rate.

los.lo: Explain the stabiliser as the means to satisfy the condition of nullifying the total sum of the moments about the lateral axis.
los.title: The stabiliser balances pitch
los.html:
Theory & physics

The wing's lift and camber moment do not act at the CG, so the tailplane provides the force that makes the total pitching moment about the CG zero.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Tailplane = pitch balance and stability.

los.lo: Explain the influence of the location of the wing CP relative to the CG on the magnitude and direction of the balancing force on the stabiliser.
los.title: Wing CP, CG and the tail load
los.html:
Theory & physics

With the CG ahead of the wing's CP (normal), the wing's lift and camber moment pitch the nose down, so the tail pushes down (negative load). The further the CP is behind the CG, the larger the down-load. A CG behind the CP needs an upward tail load.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Normal case: tail load is downwards.

los.lo: Explain the influence of the indicated airspeed on the magnitude and direction of the balancing force on the stabiliser.
los.title: IAS and the tail balancing force
los.html:
Theory & physics

At low speed (high CL) the wing CP is further forward and the tail needs less down-load; at high speed the CP moves aft and the camber moment, growing with q, needs more.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Higher IAS → larger tail down-load.

los.lo: Explain the use of the elevator deflection or stabiliser angle for the generation of the balancing force and its direction.
los.title: Elevator and stabiliser angle
los.html:
Theory & physics

The balancing force is set by changing the tail's angle of attack: elevator deflection or stabiliser incidence (trim). The tail force can be down or up depending on speed and CG.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trimmable stabiliser = balancing without holding elevator.

los.lo: Explain the elevator deflection required to balance thrust change as a function of engine position.
los.title: Thrust changes and engine position
los.html:
Theory & physics

Engines below the CG (under-wing) pitch the nose up with more thrust → nose-down elevator/trim. Engines above the CG (high tail-mounted) pitch down with more thrust → nose-up elevator.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Under-wing engines + thrust = nose-up.

los.lo: Discuss the effect of the CG location on pitch manoeuvrability and longitudinal stability.
los.title: CG, manoeuvrability and stability
los.html:
Theory & physics

Forward CG: short wing arm, long tail arm → more stable, less manoeuvrable, heavy forces, large elevator deflections. Aft CG: less stable, more manoeuvrable, light forces, until stability vanishes.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Forward CG = stable and heavy; aft CG = light and less stable.

los.lo: Define ‘neutral point’.
los.title: Neutral point
los.html:
Theory & physics

The neutral point is the CG position giving neutral static longitudinal stability: the aerodynamic centre of the whole aircraft, about which total pitching moment doesn't change with α.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • CG at NP → neutral stability.

los.lo: Explain why the location of the neutral point is only dependent on the aerodynamic design of the aeroplane.
los.title: Why the NP depends only on design
los.html:
Theory & physics

The NP is fixed by the aerodynamic design: wing AC, tail size and arm, tail lift-curve slope, downwash, fuselage. Loading moves the CG, not the NP.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Loading changes stability by moving the CG relative to a fixed NP.

los.lo: Describe the location of the neutral point relative to the locations of the aerodynamic centre of the wing and tail.
los.title: Location of the neutral point
los.html:
Theory & physics

The NP lies between the wing AC and the tail AC, normally a little behind the wing AC. A larger tail or longer tail arm moves it aft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Bigger tail → NP further aft → more stable range.

los.lo: Explain the influence of the CG location on the static longitudinal stability of the aeroplane.
los.title: CG and static longitudinal stability
los.html:
Theory & physics

Stable while the CG is ahead of the NP; the further ahead, the more stable. CG at the NP: neutral; behind it: unstable.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • CG forward of NP = stable.

los.lo: Explain the CG forward and aft limits with respect to: longitudinal control forces; elevator effectiveness; stability.
los.title: Forward and aft CG limits
los.html:
Theory & physics

Forward limit: control: the elevator must still be able to rotate for take-off and flare for landing (flaps out, near the ground); forces very heavy; stall speed and drag rise. Aft limit: stability: CG must stay sufficiently ahead of the NP to keep positive stability and a minimum stick force per g.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Forward = elevator authority; aft = stability.

los.lo: Define ‘static margin’.
los.title: Static margin
los.html:
Theory & physics

The static margin is the distance between the CG and the neutral point, usually as % MAC. Larger = more stable.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Static margin shrinks as the CG moves aft.

los.lo: Describe the Cm-alpha graph with respect to the relationship between the slope of the graph and static stability.
los.title: The Cm–α graph
los.html:
Theory & physics

Cm (nose-up positive) against α. Where it crosses Cm = 0 the aircraft is trimmed. A negative slope (more α → nose-down moment) = stable; steeper = more stable; zero slope = neutral; positive = unstable.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Stable = negative slope.

los.lo: Explain: the effect on the Cm-alpha graph of a shift of CG in the forward and aft direction; the effect on the Cm-alpha graph when the elevator is moved up or down; the effect on the Cm-alpha graph when the trim is moved; the effect of the wing contribution; the tail contribution.
los.title: What changes the Cm–α line
los.html:
Theory & physics

CG aft: slope less negative (flat at NP); CG forward: steeper. Elevator up: line moves up, same slope, trims at higher α (lower speed); down moves it down. Trim: same as elevator, shifts line, no slope change. Wing: stabilising if CG ahead of its AC, destabilising behind; camber shifts the line down. Tail: strongly stabilising (steep negative slope).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • CG changes the slope; elevator and trim change the position.

topics.title: The stick force versus speed graph (IAS)

los.lo: Explain how a pilot perceives stable static longitudinal stick force stability regarding changes in: speed; altitude; mass distribution (CG location).
los.title: Stick force stability
los.html:
Theory & physics

Trimmed in a stable aircraft: flying slower needs a pull, faster a push, and releasing the column returns it towards trim speed. Gradient is steeper with a forward CG, shallower aft; broadly similar with altitude at the same IAS (Mach/aeroelastic effects aside). Moving mass aft makes forces lighter.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Positive stick-force stability: pull to slow down.

topics.title: The manoeuvring stability/stick force per g

los.lo: Define the ‘stick force per g’, and describe that the stick force increases linearly with increase in g.
los.title: Stick force per g
los.html:
Theory & physics

The stick force per g is the pull needed to increase load factor by 1 g. In a stable aircraft the stick force increases linearly with g.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Linear relationship with load factor.

los.lo: Explain why: the stick force per g has a prescribed minimum and maximum value; the stick force per g decreases with pressure altitude.
los.title: Limits and altitude effect on stick force per g
los.html:
Theory & physics

It has a prescribed minimum (else the pilot could overstress the aircraft with a light pull) and maximum (else manoeuvring is tiring and sluggish). It decreases with pressure altitude because pitch damping, dependent on density, falls.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Higher altitude → lower stick force per g.

topics.title: Factors affecting the manoeuvring stability/stick force per g

los.lo: Explain the influence on stick force per g of: CG location; trim setting.
los.title: CG, trim and stick force per g
los.html:
Theory & physics

An aft CG reduces stick force per g; at the manoeuvre point (slightly aft of the NP) it becomes zero. Trim does not change stick force per g.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trim changes where force is zero, not the gradient.

los.lo: Describe the phugoid and short-period motion in terms of period, damping, variations (if applicable) in speed, altitude, and alpha.
los.title: Phugoid and short period
los.html:
Theory & physics

Phugoid: slow exchange of speed and height at nearly constant α, period about a minute or more, lightly damped but easy to correct. Short period: rapid pitching with large changes in α and load factor at nearly constant speed, period 1–2 s, normally heavily damped.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Phugoid: speed varies, α constant. Short period: α varies, speed constant.

los.lo: Explain why the short-period motion is more hazardous than the phugoid.
los.title: Why the short period is more hazardous
los.html:
Theory & physics

Its period is close to the pilot's reaction time, so inputs arrive late and reinforce it; its large changes in α and g can overstress the structure or stall the wing.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Fast + big α/g changes = dangerous.

los.lo: Describe ‘pilot-induced oscillations’.
los.title: Pilot-induced oscillations
los.html:
Theory & physics

A PIO is an oscillation in pitch (or roll) sustained or amplified by the pilot's own inputs, each correction arriving too late. Cure: relax or freeze the controls and let natural damping stop it.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Don't chase it; release.

los.lo: Explain the effect of high altitude on dynamic stability.
los.title: High altitude and dynamic stability
los.html:
Theory & physics

Lower density reduces aerodynamic damping in pitch, roll and yaw, so oscillations are less damped at high altitude.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Altitude → less damping.

los.lo: Describe the influence of the CG location on the dynamic longitudinal stability of the aeroplane.
los.title: CG and dynamic longitudinal stability
los.html:
Theory & physics

An aft CG reduces static stability and the damping of the short period, and makes the phugoid lightly damped or unstable; at or behind the NP the motion diverges. A forward CG improves damping.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Aft CG → poorer damping of both modes.

topics.title: Definition and effects of static directional stability

los.lo: Define ‘static directional stability’.
los.title: Static directional stability
los.html:
Theory & physics

The tendency, after a yaw disturbance, to return to flying nose into the relative airflow: weathercock stability.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • It aligns with the airflow, not with a heading.

los.lo: Explain the effects of static directional stability being too weak or too strong.
los.title: Too weak or too strong directional stability
los.html:
Theory & physics

Too weak: wanders in yaw, slips in turbulence, prone to Dutch roll. Too strong (with weak lateral stability): tends to spiral dive; harder crosswind landings (turns into wind).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Strong directional + weak lateral = spiral.

los.lo: Define ‘sideslip angle’.
los.title: Sideslip angle
los.html:
Theory & physics

The sideslip angle is the angle between the longitudinal axis and the relative airflow, seen from above.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Sideslip = flying partly sideways.

los.lo: Identify beta as the symbol used for the sideslip angle.
los.title: Symbol for sideslip
los.html:
Theory & physics

Sideslip angle symbol: β (beta).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • β = sideslip; φ = bank; α = angle of attack.

los.lo: Define the ‘yawing-moment coefficient Cn’.
los.title: Yawing-moment coefficient Cn
los.html:
Theory & physics

Cn = yawing moment about the normal axis ÷ (dynamic pressure × wing area × span).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Dimensionless; uses span as the reference length.

los.lo: Define the relationship between Cn and beta for an aeroplane with static directional stability.
los.title: Cn and β for a stable aircraft
los.html:
Theory & physics

For a directionally stable aircraft, sideslip produces a yawing moment turning the nose into the relative wind, reducing β: Cn grows with β in the restoring sense.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Restoring moment reduces sideslip.

los.lo: Explain why: Cn depends on beta; Cn equals zero for that beta that provides static equilibrium about the aeroplane’s normal axis; if no asymmetric engine thrust, flight control or loading condition prevails, the equilibrium beta equals zero.
los.title: Why Cn depends on β
los.html:
Theory & physics

Sideslip presents the fin and fuselage at an angle to the flow, so Cn depends on β. Cn = 0 at the equilibrium β; with no asymmetric thrust, control or loading, that β = 0.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Asymmetric thrust → equilibrium at a non-zero β.

los.lo: Identify how the slope of the Cn-beta graph is a measure for static directional stability.
los.title: Slope of Cn–β = directional stability
los.html:
Theory & physics

The slope of the Cn–β line measures static directional stability: the steeper the restoring slope, the more stable.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Steeper slope = more stable.

los.lo: Identify how the slope of the Cn-beta graph is affected by altitude.
los.title: Altitude and the Cn–β slope
los.html:
Theory & physics

At high altitude / high Mach the fin's lift-curve slope falls and damping is lower, so the effective slope and directional stability are reduced.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Altitude → less directional stability.

los.lo: Describe how the following aeroplane components contribute to static directional stability: wing; fin; dorsal fin; ventral fin; angle of sweep of the wing; angle of sweep of the fin; fuselage at high alpha; strakes.
los.title: Contributions to directional stability
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wing: small; sweepback stabilising (forward wing has more drag). Fin: main stabiliser (side force far behind CG). Dorsal fin: delays fin stall at large β, adds side area. Ventral fin: side area aft, helpful at high α. Fin sweep: longer arm, higher stalling β. Fuselage: forward part destabilising; forebody vortices change it at high α. Strakes: control forebody vortices or add aft side area.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Forward fuselage is destabilising directionally.
  • Dorsal fin = prevents fin stall at large sideslip.

los.lo: Explain the reduction in static directional stability when the CG moves aft.
los.title: Aft CG and directional stability
los.html:
Theory & physics

An aft CG shortens the fin's arm, reducing directional stability and rudder power.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Aft CG → less fin moment arm.

topics.title: Definition and effects of static lateral stability

los.lo: Define ‘static lateral stability’.
los.title: Static lateral stability
los.html:
Theory & physics

The tendency, after a roll disturbance, to return to wings level. Strictly the aircraft responds to the sideslip the bank causes.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Lateral stability works through sideslip.

los.lo: Explain the effects of static lateral stability being too weak or too strong.
los.title: Too weak or too strong lateral stability
los.html:
Theory & physics

Too weak: drifts into bank and turn after every gust. Too strong: rolls hard with every sideslip: harder crosswind handling, reduced roll response, promotes Dutch roll.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Strong lateral + weak directional = Dutch roll.

los.lo: Define ‘bank angle phi’.
los.title: Bank angle
los.html:
Theory & physics

Bank angle φ (phi) is the angle between the lateral axis and the horizontal, measured about the longitudinal axis.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • φ = bank.

los.lo: Define the ‘roll-moment coefficient Cl’.
los.title: Rolling-moment coefficient Cl
los.html:
Theory & physics

Cl = rolling moment about the longitudinal axis ÷ (dynamic pressure × wing area × span).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Don't confuse with CL (lift coefficient).

los.lo: Explain how without coordination the bank angle (phi) creates sideslip angle (beta).
los.title: Bank creates sideslip
los.html:
Theory & physics

Uncoordinated, a bank tilts the lift; its horizontal part pulls the aircraft sideways toward the lower wing: it slips, with β and relative wind from the low side.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Bank without rudder → slip towards the low wing.

los.lo: Describe the Cl-beta graph.
los.title: The Cl–β graph
los.html:
Theory & physics

In a sideslip, a laterally stable aircraft produces a rolling moment that raises the lower (leading) wing. The curve passes through zero at zero sideslip.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Restoring roll raises the into-wind wing.

los.lo: Identify the slope of the Cl-beta graph as a measure for static lateral stability.
los.title: Slope of Cl–β = lateral stability
los.html:
Theory & physics

The slope of the Cl–β curve measures static lateral stability: steeper = more stable.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Same logic as Cn–β for yaw.

los.lo: Identify how the slope of the Cl-beta graph is affected by altitude.
los.title: Altitude and the Cl–β slope
los.html:
Theory & physics

The effective slope falls at high altitude: lower damping and changed response.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Altitude → less effective lateral stability.

los.lo: Explain the contribution to the static lateral stability of: dihedral, anhedral; high wing, low wing; sweep angle of the wing; ventral fin; vertical tail.
los.title: Contributions to lateral stability
los.html:
Theory & physics

Dihedral: forward (low) wing meets the air at higher α, gains lift → stabilising; anhedral destabilising. High wing: fuselage crossflow raises forward-wing root α → stabilising (with low CG; often given anhedral); low wing destabilising, needs more dihedral. Sweepback: forward wing effectively less swept → more lift → strongly stabilising, more at high CL. Ventral fin: below the roll axis → destabilising. Vertical tail: above the roll axis → stabilising.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • High wing + sweep often get anhedral to avoid excess stability.
  • Ventral fin: stabilising directionally, destabilising laterally.

los.lo: Explain how lateral and directional stability are coupled.
los.title: Lateral–directional coupling
los.html:
Theory & physics

Roll and yaw are coupled: bank → sideslip; sideslip → yaw (directional stability) and roll (lateral stability); yaw → wing speed difference → roll. They never occur alone.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Every bank produces yaw, and every yaw produces roll.

los.lo: Explain how high static directional stability and low static lateral stability may cause spiral divergence (unstable spiral dive), and under which conditions the spiral dive mode is neutral or stable.
los.title: Cause of spiral divergence
los.html:
Theory & physics

Strong directional, weak lateral stability: after a small bank and sideslip, the fin yaws the nose into the turn faster than the wings roll level; the faster outer wing gains lift and steepens the bank. Better balance gives a neutral (constant bank) or stable (wings return level) spiral mode.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Spiral divergence: directional > lateral.

los.lo: Describe an unstable spiral dive mode with respect to deviations in speed, bank angle, nose low-pitch attitude, and decreasing altitude.
los.title: The unstable spiral dive
los.html:
Theory & physics

Speed increases, bank increases, nose drops lower, height loss accelerates. Slow to develop: dangerous when distracted or in cloud. Recovery: reduce power, roll wings level first, then ease out of the dive.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Level the wings before pulling.

los.lo: Describe Dutch roll.
los.title: Dutch roll
los.html:
Theory & physics

Dutch roll is a combined oscillating yaw and roll: the aircraft yaws one way and rolls the other, repeatedly, with a period of a few seconds; the wing tips trace ellipses.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Yaw and roll out of phase.

los.lo: Explain: why Dutch roll occurs when the static lateral stability is higher than static directional stability; the conditions for a stable, neutral or unstable Dutch roll motion; the function of the yaw damper; the actions to be taken when the yaw damper is not available.
los.title: Dutch roll causes, yaw damper and actions
los.html:
Theory & physics

Occurs when lateral stability is strong relative to directional: yaw → sideslip → strong roll; fin yaws back, overshoots; repeat. Swept wings at altitude are prone. More directional stability/damping → stable; less → neutral or unstable. A yaw damper senses yaw rate and moves the rudder against it. Yaw damper inoperative: fly lower and slower per AFM; damp with small, well-timed aileron inputs (not rudder) or follow the type procedure.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Dutch roll: lateral > directional.
  • Yaw damper uses the rudder.

los.lo: Describe how the asymmetric nature of shock waves on both wings, at high Mach numbers, can lead to Dutch roll.
los.title: Shock waves and Dutch roll
los.html:
Theory & physics

At high Mach, sideslip changes the effective sweep of each wing: the shock is stronger on one side, giving asymmetric lift and drag, adding roll and yaw moments that can start or worsen Dutch roll.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Asymmetric shocks feed Dutch roll at high Mach.

topics.title: Effects of altitude on dynamic stability

los.lo: Explain that increased pressure altitude reduces dynamic lateral/directional stability.
los.title: Altitude and lateral/directional dynamics
los.html:
Theory & physics

Higher pressure altitude → lower density → less aerodynamic damping with unchanged inertia, so Dutch roll and the other lateral/directional modes are less damped.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Yaw damper matters most at altitude.

topics.title: Basics - The three planes and three axes

los.lo: Define: lateral axis; longitudinal axis; normal axis.
los.title: The three axes
los.html:
Theory & physics

All pass through the CG at right angles: lateral (tip to tip, pitch), longitudinal (nose to tail, roll), normal (vertical, yaw).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Pitch about the lateral axis.

los.lo: Define: pitch angle; bank angle (PHI); yaw angle.
los.title: Pitch, bank and yaw angles
los.html:
Theory & physics

Pitch angle: longitudinal axis vs horizontal. Bank angle φ: lateral axis vs horizontal. Yaw angle: longitudinal axis vs a horizontal reference direction (e.g. original heading).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Bank is measured with the lateral axis.

los.lo: Describe the motion about the three axes.
los.title: Motion about the three axes
los.html:
Theory & physics

Pitch: nose up/down. Roll: one wing down, the other up. Yaw: nose left/right.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Each motion is a rotation about the CG.

los.lo: Name and describe the devices that control these motions.
los.title: Primary flight controls
los.html:
Theory & physics

Elevator (or all-moving tailplane) → pitch. Ailerons (helped by roll spoilers) → roll. Rudder → yaw.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Roll spoilers assist the ailerons.

los.lo: State that camber is changed by movement of a control surface and explain the effect.
los.title: Control surfaces change camber
los.html:
Theory & physics

Deflecting a trailing-edge surface down adds camber and increases lift; up reduces or reverses camber and decreases lift.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Control surface = variable camber.

los.lo: Explain the influence of local alpha change by movement of a control surface.
los.title: Control surfaces change local α
los.html:
Theory & physics

Deflection tilts the effective chord line: down deflection increases the section's effective α, up reduces it. That is why a down aileron near the stall can stall that wing.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Down aileron near the stall → more α → wing may stall.

los.lo: Explain the working principle of the elevator/all-flying tail and describe its function.
los.title: Elevator and all-flying tail
los.html:
Theory & physics

The elevator changes the tailplane's camber and lift; with a long arm behind the CG, small forces give large pitching moments. Pull back → elevator up → less tail lift (more down-load) → nose up. An all-flying tail moves the whole surface: more powerful and effective at high Mach where a shock ahead of a hinged elevator would weaken it.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Stick back = elevator up = nose up.

los.lo: Explain the effect of downwash on the tailplane alpha.
los.title: Downwash and tailplane α
los.html:
Theory & physics

The tail sits in the wing's downwash, so its α is less than the aircraft's by the downwash angle. Flap extension, α changes or ground effect change the downwash and so the tail α and pitching moment, which must be trimmed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • More downwash → tail α more negative.

los.lo: Explain the relationship between elevator deflection and CG location to produce a given aeroplane response.
los.title: Elevator deflection and CG
los.html:
Theory & physics

Forward CG: very stable, so more elevator deflection and force for a given response. Aft CG: less deflection needed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Forward CG = more elevator for the same manoeuvre.

los.lo: Explain the effect of forward CG limit on pitch control.
los.title: Forward CG limit and pitch control
los.html:
Theory & physics

The forward CG limit is where full elevator can only just achieve rotation at take-off and the flare at landing speed with full flap in ground effect (the hardest case).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Most critical: landing flare, full flap, in ground effect.

los.lo: Describe the effect of engine thrust on pitching moments for different engine locations.
los.title: Thrust and pitch for different engine positions
los.html:
Theory & physics

Low-mounted (under-wing) engines: thrust increase → nose-up, reduction → nose-down. High-mounted (rear fuselage or over-wing): the opposite. Strongest at low speed with big thrust changes, e.g. go-around.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Go-around with under-wing engines → strong pitch-up.

los.lo: Explain the working principle of the rudder and describe its function. State the relationship between rudder deflection and the moment about the normal axis. Describe the effect of sideslip on the moment about the normal axis.
los.title: Rudder
los.html:
Theory & physics

The rudder changes the fin's camber and side force, yawing the aircraft; moment grows with deflection and dynamic pressure. The resulting sideslip makes the fin produce an opposing restoring moment, balancing the rudder at a steady sideslip angle.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Constant rudder → steady sideslip, not continuous yaw.

los.lo: Explain why and how rudder deflection is limited on CAT aeroplanes.
los.title: Rudder limiting on transport aircraft
los.html:
Theory & physics

At high speed full rudder would overload the fin, so travel is limited with airspeed (ratio changer / travel limiter). Large alternating rudder inputs can still overload the fin and must be avoided.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Avoid rudder reversals at any speed.

los.lo: Explain the functioning of ailerons.
los.title: How ailerons work
los.html:
Theory & physics

Ailerons on the outer trailing edges move oppositely: the down aileron increases lift on its wing, the up aileron reduces it; the aircraft rolls towards the up aileron.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Roll is towards the up aileron.

los.lo: Describe the adverse effects of aileron deflection. (Refer to Subjects 081 05 04 04 and 081 06 01 02)
los.title: Adverse effects of aileron deflection
los.html:
Theory & physics

Aileron deflection causes adverse yaw and twists the wing, which at high speed can reduce or reverse its effect.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Two problems: adverse yaw and aeroelastic twist.

los.lo: Explain why some aeroplanes have inboard and outboard ailerons.
los.title: Inboard and outboard ailerons
los.html:
Theory & physics

At low speed both are used for maximum roll power. At high speed only the stiffer inboard ailerons are used, because outboard ones near the flexible tips would twist the wing too much.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • High speed: inboard only.

los.lo: State that the outboard ailerons are locked beyond a given speed to prevent: over-control; exceeding structural limitations; aeroelastic phenomena (flutter, divergence and aileron reversal).
los.title: Outboard aileron lockout
los.html:
Theory & physics

Outboard ailerons are locked out above a set speed (or with flaps up) to prevent over-control, structural overload, and aeroelastic effects: flutter, divergence and aileron reversal (wing twist cancelling or reversing the aileron's effect).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Aileron reversal = wing twist overrides the aileron.

los.lo: Describe the use of aileron deflection in normal flight, flight with sideslip, crosswind landings, horizontal turns, flight with one-engine-inoperative.
los.title: Aileron use in different flight conditions
los.html:
Theory & physics

Normal flight: enter/exit turns, hold wings level. Sideslip: hold bank against the roll from lateral stability. Crosswind landing: into wind. Turns: roll in/out; sometimes slight opposite aileron to stop overbanking. One engine inoperative: hold a small bank towards the live engine.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • OEI: bank towards the live engine.
  • Crosswind: aileron into wind.

los.lo: Define ‘roll rate’.
los.title: Roll rate
los.html:
Theory & physics

Roll rate is the angular velocity about the longitudinal axis, in °/s.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Rate, not angle.

los.lo: List the factors that affect roll rate.
los.title: Factors affecting roll rate
los.html:
Theory & physics

Aileron deflection and size; dynamic pressure (IAS); TAS (with roll damping, steady roll rate ∝ TAS for a given deflection); span (more damping and inertia); aeroelastic wing twist.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Longer span → lower roll rate.

los.lo: Describe flaperons and aileron droop.
los.title: Flaperons and aileron droop
los.html:
Theory & physics

Flaperons act as flaps (both down) and ailerons (differential). Aileron droop lowers both ailerons slightly with flaps extended, so the whole trailing edge adds lift.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Droop = more lift, not roll.

los.lo: Explain how spoilers can be used to control the rolling movement in combination with or instead of the ailerons.
los.title: Roll spoilers
los.html:
Theory & physics

Roll spoilers rise on the wing that must go down, reducing its lift and adding drag. Used with the ailerons or, at high speed with outboard ailerons locked, partly instead of them. They don't twist the wing, and their drag gives a favourable yaw.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Spoiler up on the down-going wing.

los.lo: Explain why the use of ailerons induces adverse yaw.
los.title: Adverse yaw
los.html:
Theory & physics

The down aileron increases its wing's lift and induced drag; the extra drag on the rising wing yaws the nose away from the turn. Strongest at low speed, high CL.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Adverse yaw = nose yaws opposite to the roll.

los.lo: Explain how the following reduce adverse yaw: Frise ailerons; differential aileron deflection; rudder aileron cross-coupling; roll spoilers.
los.title: Reducing adverse yaw
los.html:
Theory & physics

Frise ailerons: the up aileron's nose projects below the wing, adding drag on the descending wing. Differential ailerons: up aileron moves further than down. Rudder–aileron interconnect: rudder applied automatically. Roll spoilers: drag on the descending wing.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • All work by adding drag on the down-going wing.

los.lo: Explain the secondary effect of roll.
los.title: Secondary effect of roll
los.html:
Theory & physics

A bank makes the aircraft slip towards the lower wing; directional stability then yaws the nose towards the lower wing. Roll → yaw.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Roll left → yaw left.

los.lo: Explain the secondary effect of yaw.
los.title: Secondary effect of yaw
los.html:
Theory & physics

Yaw speeds up the outer wing (more lift), and sideslip via lateral stability raises the leading wing: the aircraft rolls in the direction of yaw. Yaw → roll.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Yaw right → roll right.

los.lo: Describe the purpose of aerodynamic balance.
los.title: Purpose of aerodynamic balance
los.html:
Theory & physics

Control force depends on the hinge moment. Aerodynamic balance puts part of the surface area or force ahead of the hinge, where the air helps move the surface, reducing pilot force.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Too much balance → overbalance (surface runs away).

los.lo: Describe the working principle of the horn balance.
los.title: Horn balance
los.html:
Theory & physics

Part of the surface, usually at its tip, extends ahead of the hinge line; air pressure on it helps deflect the surface.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Horn = area forward of the hinge.

los.lo: Describe the working principle of the internal balance.
los.title: Internal balance
los.html:
Theory & physics

A plate ahead of the hinge sits inside a sealed chamber; the pressure difference between upper and lower surfaces acts on it and helps move the surface.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • No external protrusion; uses the pressure difference.

los.lo: Describe the working principle and application of: balance tab; anti-balance tab; spring tab; servo tab.
los.title: Balance, anti-balance, spring and servo tabs
los.html:
Theory & physics

Balance tab: moves opposite to the surface, reduces pilot force. Anti-balance tab: moves the same way, increases force (feel for over-light controls, e.g. all-moving tail). Servo tab: pilot moves only the tab; its force moves a free-floating surface. Spring tab: via a spring; little help at low speed, more as loads rise.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Same direction = anti-balance.
  • Servo tab: pilot drives the tab, not the surface.

los.lo: State the differences between fully powered controls and power-assisted controls.
los.title: Fully powered versus power-assisted
los.html:
Theory & physics

Power-assisted: pilot moves the surface via linkage, hydraulics add force, pilot feels part of the load. Fully powered: actuators do everything; pilot feels no aerodynamic load (irreversible).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Fully powered = no natural feel.

los.lo: Describe power-assisted controls.
los.title: Power-assisted controls
los.html:
Theory & physics

Mechanical linkage plus hydraulic jacks that add force; the pilot feels a fraction of the real aerodynamic load.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Feel is reduced but still natural.

los.lo: Describe the advantages of artificial feel in fully powered control.
los.title: Artificial feel
los.html:
Theory & physics

Fully powered controls get artificial feel (springs, q-feel increasing with dynamic pressure). It gives a sense of speed and load, prevents over-controlling and overstressing.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • q-feel: force rises with IAS.

los.lo: Explain which parameters may be controlled in level flight with the pitch control law.
los.title: FBW pitch control law
los.html:
Theory & physics

The stick commands load factor or pitch rate (or a blend), not elevator deflection. Stick released: the aircraft holds its flight path and trims automatically for speed, configuration and thrust changes.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Neutral stick = hold flight path.

los.lo: Explain the advantages of using the CG position in the FBW system.
los.title: CG in the FBW system
los.html:
Theory & physics
