Knowing the CG, the computers can keep handling the same at every CG, permit an aft CG and smaller tail (relaxed stability, less drag), and use CG in protections and tail-fuel transfer.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Benefit: less trim drag, consistent handling.

los.lo: Explain what type of flight-degraded control laws may be available in case of failure.
los.title: Degraded control laws
los.html:
Theory & physics

After failures: alternate law (fewer protections) or direct law (stick → surface directly, manual trim). Last resort: mechanical backup.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Direct law = conventional-aircraft behaviour.

los.lo: Explain what are hard and soft protections.
los.title: Hard and soft protections
los.html:
Theory & physics

Protections cover α, load factor, attitude and overspeed. Hard: the pilot cannot exceed the limit whatever the input (Airbus). Soft: forces increase or warnings sound near the limit but the pilot can exceed it with more force (Boeing).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Hard = cannot override.

los.lo: State the reasons for using trimming devices.
los.title: Why trim
los.html:
Theory & physics

Trim removes the steady force needed to hold an attitude or speed after changes in speed, configuration, power or CG, reducing fatigue and improving accuracy.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trim sets zero stick force.

los.lo: Explain the difference between a trim tab and the various balance tabs.
los.title: Trim tab versus balance tab
los.html:
Theory & physics

A trim tab is set independently by the pilot/autopilot and stays put: it sets the zero-force condition. A balance tab moves automatically with the surface: it changes the force per deflection without changing the trimmed condition.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Trim tab: independent. Balance tab: geared to the surface.

los.lo: Describe the working principle of a trim tab including cockpit indications.
los.title: Trim tab operation and indication
los.html:
Theory & physics

Moving the tab one way makes the surface float the other way: for nose-up trim (elevator up) the tab moves down. A cockpit indicator shows the setting (nose-up/nose-down).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Nose-up trim → tab down.

los.lo: Describe the working principle of a stabiliser trim including the flight deck indications.
los.title: Stabiliser trim
los.html:
Theory & physics

Jets move the whole trimmable horizontal stabiliser (motor and screwjack); once trimmed the elevator streamlines with it. Indicator in units or degrees with a green band for take-off.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • THS changes the stabiliser incidence.

los.lo: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of a stabiliser trim compared to a trim tab.
los.title: Stabiliser trim versus trim tab
los.html:
Theory & physics

Advantages: much larger trim range; elevator stays streamlined (less drag) with full travel available. Disadvantages: heavier, more complex; runaway or jam is far more serious (very powerful surface).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Big advantage: elevator authority preserved.

los.lo: Explain the relationship between CG position, take-off trim setting, and stabiliser trim position.
los.title: CG and take-off stabiliser setting
los.html:
Theory & physics

Forward CG → more nose-up stabiliser trim; aft CG → less. Calculated from the load-sheet CG (sometimes thrust and flap); a take-off configuration warning sounds outside the green band.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Forward CG = more nose-up trim.

los.lo: Explain the effect of errors in the take-off stabiliser trim setting on the rotation characteristics and stick force during take-off rotation.
los.title: Take-off trim errors
los.html:
Theory & physics

Too nose-down (or CG further aft than assumed): heavy pull, slow rotation, delayed lift-off, longer run. Too nose-up (or CG further forward than assumed): early or self-rotation, over-rotation, tail strike, lift-off too slow.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Mis-set nose-up → tail strike risk.

los.lo: Discuss the effects of jammed and runaway stabiliser.
los.title: Runaway and jammed stabiliser
los.html:
Theory & physics

Runaway: continuous uncommanded movement, rapidly growing out-of-trim force → stop it at once with the trim cut-out switches, then trim manually if possible. Jammed: stuck at one setting.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Runaway: cut-out switches first.

los.lo: Explain the consequences of a jammed stabiliser during take-off, landing, and go-around.
los.title: Jammed stabiliser in take-off, landing and go-around
los.html:
Theory & physics

Take-off: jammed outside the green band → abnormal rotation forces. Landing: jammed at a cruise setting → very large elevator forces as speed falls and flaps extend; use higher approach speed, reduced flap, care in the flare. Go-around: thrust and configuration changes give large pitch changes the elevator may struggle to hold.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Jammed at cruise setting: landing needs reduced flap, higher speed.

los.lo: Describe the phenomenon of flutter and how IAS and mass distribution affects the likelihood of flutter occurrence.
los.title: Flutter
los.html:
Theory & physics

Flutter is a self-sustaining, rapidly growing oscillation where aerodynamic, elastic and inertial forces feed each other (bending ↔ twisting ↔ control-surface lag). Above the flutter speed it can destroy the structure in seconds. More likely with higher IAS and a centre of mass behind the hinge line or elastic axis.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Driven by IAS (dynamic pressure).
  • CG of a control surface aft of the hinge promotes flutter.

los.lo: Describe the use of mass balance to alleviate the flutter problem by adjusting the mass distribution: wing-mounted engines on pylons; control surface mass balance.
los.title: Mass balance against flutter
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wing engines on pylons are placed ahead of the wing's elastic axis to damp bending–torsion coupling. Control surfaces carry balance weights ahead of the hinge line so their centre of mass is on or ahead of it.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Balance mass goes forward of the hinge.

los.lo: Explain what is the flight envelope free of flutter.
los.title: Flutter-free envelope
los.html:
Theory & physics

The aircraft is designed and tested to be flutter-free throughout the envelope up to VD/MD with a margin (≈ 1.2 VD). Damaged balance weights, loose surfaces, excess play or extra paint can bring the flutter speed into the normal envelope.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Repainting a control surface can unbalance it.

los.lo: Describe the reason for flap/landing gear limitations. Define ‘VLO’. Define ‘VLE’.
los.title: Gear and flap limits, VLO and VLE
los.html:
Theory & physics

Gear and flaps can't take high-speed loads. VLO: max speed to extend or retract the gear. VLE: max speed to fly with gear extended (and locked).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • VLO = operating; VLE = extended.

los.lo: Explain why there is a difference between VLO and VLE in the case of some aeroplane types.
los.title: Why VLO can be lower than VLE
los.html:
Theory & physics

During transit the doors are open and the gear is unlocked and moving, so actuators and doors can take less load than the locked, extended gear.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Usually VLO ≤ VLE.

los.lo: Define ‘VFE’ and describe flap limiting speeds.
los.title: VFE
los.html:
Theory & physics

VFE is the max speed with flaps in a given extended position. Each setting has its own VFE, lower for larger settings, set by flap and mechanism strength.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • More flap → lower VFE.

los.lo: Describe flap design features, procedures and warnings to prevent overload.
los.title: Protecting flaps from overload
los.html:
Theory & physics

Placards and markings (white arc on light aircraft), flap load relief (auto-retracts to a smaller setting above VFE, re-extends when slower), overspeed warnings, and procedures requiring speed below the next setting's VFE before selecting it.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Load relief retracts flaps automatically.

los.lo: Define ‘VMO’, ‘VNO’, and ‘VNE’.
los.title: VMO, VNO and VNE
los.html:
Theory & physics

VNO (CS-23): max structural cruising speed; exceed only in smooth air, with caution; top of the green arc; ≤ VC. VNE (CS-23): never exceed, red line; ≤ 0.9 VD. VMO (CS-25/turbine): max IAS not to be deliberately exceeded in any phase; ≤ VC.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • VNE ≤ 0.9 VD.

los.lo: Explain the significance of VMO, VNO and VNE, and the differences between these airspeeds.
los.title: Significance of VMO, VNO, VNE
los.html:
Theory & physics

VNO marks a caution range where gusts could overstress the structure. VNE and VMO are hard limits keeping a margin below VD, where flutter, control and structural problems arise.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Yellow arc = between VNO and VNE: smooth air only.

los.lo: Explain the hazards of flying at speeds above VNE and VMO.
los.title: Hazards above VNE and VMO
los.html:
Theory & physics

Loads above limit (especially in gusts or manoeuvres), flutter and aeroelastic effects, reduced or reversed control, damage to doors, fairings and windscreens, and loss of the design margin to VD.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Main danger: flutter and structural failure.

los.lo: Define ‘MMO’ and state its limiting factors.
los.title: MMO and its limiting factors
los.html:
Theory & physics

MMO is the Mach number not to be deliberately exceeded. Limited by high-speed buffet and shock-induced separation, Mach tuck and stability/control changes, flutter margins, and a margin below MD.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • MMO is about compressibility; VMO about dynamic pressure.

los.lo: Describe the manoeuvring-load diagram.
los.title: Manoeuvring-load diagram
los.html:
Theory & physics

The V–n diagram shows, for a given mass and configuration, the load factors the aircraft can produce and withstand against EAS. Bounded by the stall (left), limit load factors (top and bottom) and VD (right). Outside: stall or overstress.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Left boundary = stall; right = VD.

los.lo: Define limit and ultimate load factor, and explain what can happen if these values are exceeded.
los.title: Limit and ultimate load factor
los.html:
Theory & physics

Limit load: largest load expected in service; carried without permanent deformation. Ultimate load = limit × 1.5 (safety factor); carried without failure for at least 3 s, possibly with permanent deformation. Beyond limit → permanent bending; beyond ultimate → failure.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • CS-25 limit +2.5 → ultimate +3.75.

los.lo: Define ‘VA’, ‘VB’, ‘VC’, and ‘VD’.
los.title: VA, VB, VC, VD
los.html:
Theory & physics

VA: design manoeuvring speed (stalls at the positive limit n). VB: design speed for maximum gust intensity. VC: design cruising speed. VD: design diving speed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Order: VA (or VB) < VC < VD.

los.lo: Identify and explain the varying features on the VN diagram: load factor ‘n’; speed scale, equivalent airspeed; equivalent airspeed envelope; 1g stall speed; stall boundary (refer to 081 03 01 02).
los.title: Features of the V–n diagram
los.html:
Theory & physics

Vertical axis: load factor n. Horizontal: EAS (so it applies at any altitude where compressibility is negligible). Outline: stall curves, ±limit lines, VD. VS1G where the stall curve crosses n = 1. Stall boundary: n = (V/VS1G)², a parabola reaching the positive limit at VA.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Speed scale is EAS.

los.lo: Describe the relationship between VMO or VNE and VC.
los.title: VMO/VNE and VC
los.html:
Theory & physics

VMO ≤ VC for transport aircraft; VNE ≈ 0.9 VD for light aircraft, leaving a margin for upsets.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Both sit between VC and VD (VMO at most VC).

los.lo: State all the manoeuvring load-factors limits applicable to CS-23 and CS-25 aeroplanes.
los.title: CS-23 and CS-25 load factor limits
los.html:
Theory & physics

CS-25: +2.5 to −1.0 flaps up (+2.1 + 24 000/(W + 10 000) lb, between 2.5 and 3.8; −1.0 up to VC, 0 at VD); flaps out +2.0 to 0. CS-23 normal: +3.8 / −1.52. Utility: +4.4 / −1.76. Aerobatic: +6.0 / −3.0. Flaps out (all CS-23): +2.0 / 0.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Negative limit ≈ 0.4 × positive (CS-23 normal/utility); 0.5 × aerobatic.

los.lo: Explain the relationship between VA and VS in a formula, and calculate the values.
los.title: VA and VS
los.html:
Theory & physics

VA = VS1G × √nlimit. Examples: 120 kt, n 2.5 → ≈ 190 kt; 60 kt, n 3.8 → ≈ 117 kt.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Use the square root of the limit load factor.

los.lo: Explain the significance of VA and the adverse consequences of applying full, abrupt nose-up elevator deflection when exceeding VA.
los.title: Significance of VA
los.html:
Theory & physics

Below VA a full, abrupt nose-up input stalls the wing before the limit load is reached: the stall protects the structure. Above VA the same input can exceed the limit load (deformation or failure) before stalling. Even below VA, repeated or reversing inputs (especially rudder) can exceed design loads.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Below VA = protection against one full abrupt input, not reversals.

los.lo: State the relationship of mass to load-factor limits and accelerated stall speed boundary limit.
los.title: Mass, load factor limits and stall boundary
los.html:
Theory & physics

Limit load factor is per unit weight: at the same n a heavier aircraft carries a higher absolute load. The accelerated stall boundary moves to higher speeds with √mass.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Heavier → stall curve moves right.

los.lo: Calculate the change of VA with changing mass.
los.title: VA and mass
los.html:
Theory & physics

VA2 = VA1 × √(m2/m1): VA decreases at lower mass. Example: 110 kt at 1100 kg → at 880 kg ≈ 98 kt.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Lighter = lower VA (counter-intuitive exam favourite).

los.lo: Explain why VA loses significance at higher altitude.
los.title: VA at high altitude
los.html:
Theory & physics

At altitude the stall IAS rises with compressibility, high-speed buffet appears, and the envelope is bounded by Mach limits, not the EAS V–n diagram. VA may be near or above VMO; protection comes from the buffet boundaries.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • At altitude think buffet margin, not VA.

los.lo: Define ‘MC’ and ‘MD’.
los.title: MC and MD
los.html:
Theory & physics

MC: design cruising Mach number. MD: design diving Mach number. Mach equivalents of VC and VD at high altitude.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • MMO keeps a margin below MD.

los.lo: Recognise a typical gust-load diagram, and state the minimum gust speeds in ft/s, m/s and kt that the aeroplane must be designed to withstand at VB to VC and VD.
los.title: Gust-load diagram and design gusts
los.html:
Theory & physics

A vertical gust changes α, so lift and load factor. The gust-load diagram shows lines fanning out from n = 1 at zero EAS. Design gusts (EAS, up to 20 000 ft): VB: 66 ft/s (20.1 m/s, 39 kt); VC: 50 ft/s (15.2 m/s, 30 kt); VD: 25 ft/s (7.6 m/s, 15 kt).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • 66 / 50 / 25 ft/s at VB / VC / VD.

los.lo: Discuss considerations for the selection of VRA.
los.title: Choosing VRA
los.html:
Theory & physics

VRA (rough-air speed) gives a good margin against stall/low-speed buffet in strong gusts, while staying far enough below VMO/MMO that speed excursions won't exceed them; no higher than VB, close to it.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • VRA balances stall margin against overspeed margin.

los.lo: Explain the adverse effects on the aeroplane when flying in turbulence.
los.title: Effects of turbulence
los.html:
Theory & physics

Structural loads (fatigue, overstress), speed and height excursions, stall or buffet, possible loss of control, hard-to-read instruments, injuries. Fly VRA, hold attitude rather than chasing speed and height, keep belts fastened.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • In turbulence: hold attitude, not altitude.

los.lo: Describe and explain the relationship between the gust-load factor and the following: lift-curve slope, aspect ratio, angle of sweep, altitude, wing loading, weight, wing area, equivalent airspeed (EAS), and speed of vertical gust. (Note: For examination purposes, the ECQB questions will not be calculation based.)
los.title: What sets the gust load factor
los.html:
Theory & physics

Δn ∝ a × Ue × VE / (W/S). Gust load increases with a steeper lift-curve slope (higher aspect ratio; less sweep), higher EAS and stronger vertical gust. It decreases with higher wing loading: heavier aircraft or smaller wing area feel less. Altitude: no change at the same EAS; at the same TAS, less (lower density).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Light aircraft are thrown around more.
  • Sweep reduces gust response (flatter lift curve).

subs.title: Conversion of engine torque to thrust

topics.title: Explain conversion of aerodynamic force on a propeller blade

los.lo: Explain the resolution of aerodynamic force on a propeller blade element into lift and drag or into thrust and torque.
los.title: Blade forces: lift/drag or thrust/torque
los.html:
Theory & physics

Each blade element meets a relative airflow combining rotation (2πr × rpm) and TAS. Its force splits into lift and drag (relative to that airflow) or thrust (along the axis) and a torque force (in the plane of rotation, opposing rotation). Summed over the blades, the torque force × radius is the aerodynamic torque the engine must supply.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Thrust/torque are relative to the propeller axis; lift/drag to the relative airflow.

los.lo: Describe how propeller thrust and aerodynamic torque vary with IAS.
los.title: Thrust and torque versus IAS
los.html:
Theory & physics

Fixed pitch, constant rpm: as IAS rises, the airflow comes more from ahead, blade α falls, and thrust and torque fall (the engine speeds up unless throttled back). Maximum static thrust at zero airspeed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Fixed pitch: faster → less thrust, rpm rises.

los.lo: Describe the geometry of a typical propeller blade element at the reference section: blade chord line; propeller rotational velocity vector; true airspeed vector; blade angle of attack; pitch or blade angle; advance or helix angle. Define ‘geometric pitch’, ‘effective pitch’, and ‘propeller slip’. Remark: For theoretical knowledge examination purposes, the following definition is used for geometric pitch: the theoretical distance a propeller would advance in one revolution at zero blade angle of attack.
los.title: Blade element geometry, pitch and slip
los.html:
Theory & physics

At the reference section (≈ 75 % radius): chord line; rotational velocity (plane of rotation); TAS (along the axis); helix angle (relative airflow vs plane of rotation); blade angle (chord vs plane of rotation); blade α = blade angle − helix angle. Geometric pitch: advance per revolution at zero blade α. Effective pitch: actual advance per revolution. Slip = geometric − effective pitch.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Blade α = blade angle − helix angle.
  • Slip is what creates blade α and thrust.

los.lo: Describe how the terms ‘fine pitch’ and ‘coarse pitch’ can be used to express blade angle.
los.title: Fine and coarse pitch
los.html:
Theory & physics

Fine pitch = small blade angle: take-off and climb (low speed, high rpm). Coarse pitch = large blade angle: cruise (high speed, lower rpm).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Fine = small angle = high rpm.

los.lo: Define ‘blade twist’.
los.title: Blade twist
los.html:
Theory & physics

Blade twist is the decrease of blade angle from root to tip.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Blade angle is largest at the root.

los.lo: Explain why blade twist is necessary.
los.title: Why blades are twisted
los.html:
Theory & physics

Rotational speed increases with radius while forward speed is constant, so the helix angle is large at the root, small at the tip. To keep a similar efficient α along the blade, the blade angle must decrease towards the tip.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Purpose: equal α along the blade.

topics.title: Fixed pitch and variable pitch/constant speed

los.lo: List the different types of propellers: fixed pitch; adjustable pitch or variable pitch (non-governing); variable pitch (governing)/constant speed.
los.title: Types of propeller
los.html:
Theory & physics

Fixed pitch; adjustable or variable pitch (non-governing) (changed on the ground or by the pilot, not automatically); variable pitch (governing) = constant speed (governor holds selected rpm).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Constant speed = governed variable pitch.

los.lo: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of fixed-pitch and constant-speed propellers.
los.title: Fixed pitch versus constant speed
los.html:
Theory & physics

Fixed: simple, light, cheap, reliable, but efficient at one speed only. Constant speed: efficient blade α over a wide speed range, rpm and power set separately; but heavier, costlier, complex, more maintenance and workload.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Constant speed wins on efficiency range.

los.lo: Discuss climb and cruise propellers.
los.title: Climb and cruise propellers
los.html:
Theory & physics

Climb propeller: fine pitch: good take-off and climb, but overspeeds and is inefficient at high cruise. Cruise propeller: coarse pitch: efficient in cruise, poor take-off and climb.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Climb prop = fine; cruise prop = coarse.

los.lo: Explain the relationship between blade angle, blade angle of attack, and airspeed for fixed and variable pitch propellers.
los.title: Blade angle, blade α and airspeed
los.html:
Theory & physics

Fixed pitch at constant rpm: as airspeed rises the helix angle grows and blade α falls. Variable pitch: the blade angle increases with airspeed, keeping α near its best value.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Faster airspeed → larger helix angle.

los.lo: Describe and explain the forces that act on a rotating blade element in normal, feathered, windmilling, and reverse operation.
los.title: Normal, windmilling, feathered and reverse
los.html:
Theory & physics

Normal: positive blade α; forward thrust, torque opposing rotation. Windmilling: negative blade α; force points backwards (drag), torque drives the propeller. Feathered: blade angle ≈ 90°, edge-on; no rotation, minimum drag. Reverse: negative blade angle; pushes air forward for braking.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Windmilling = negative α, large drag.

los.lo: Explain the effects of changing propeller pitch at constant IAS.
los.title: Changing pitch at constant IAS
los.html:
Theory & physics

At constant IAS, coarser pitch raises blade α → more thrust and torque; at unchanged power rpm falls. Finer pitch does the opposite. The constant-speed unit coarsens pitch when rpm rises.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • CSU response to overspeed: coarsen pitch.

los.lo: Define ‘propeller efficiency’.
los.title: Propeller efficiency
los.html:
Theory & physics

η = (thrust × TAS) / shaft power: useful thrust power over power delivered.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Output uses TAS.

los.lo: Explain and describe the relationship between propeller efficiency and speed (TAS) for different types of propellers.
los.title: Efficiency versus TAS
los.html:
Theory & physics

Zero at zero TAS (despite static thrust), rising to a peak of about 80–85 %, then falling at high speed (small blade α, tip compressibility). Fixed pitch: peak at one speed. Constant speed: follows the envelope of many fixed-pitch curves, staying near peak over a wide range.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • η = 0 at brake release.

los.lo: Explain the relationship between blade angle and thrust.
los.title: Blade angle and thrust
los.html:
Theory & physics

At a given TAS and rpm, a larger blade angle gives a larger blade α and more thrust, until the blade stalls; then thrust falls and drag rises.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Blades can stall like wings.

los.lo: Describe the effects and hazards of ice on a propeller.
los.title: Ice on the propeller
los.html:
Theory & physics

Ice reduces thrust and efficiency and increases power needed; uneven build-up and shedding cause imbalance and vibration; shed ice can damage the fuselage (hence reinforced panels). Protected by electric boots or fluid.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Symptom: vibration.

los.lo: Describe the effects of an inoperative engine on the performance and controllability of an aeroplane: thrust loss/drag increase; influence on yaw moment during asymmetric power.
los.title: Inoperative engine: performance and yaw
los.html:
Theory & physics

Thrust lost plus large drag from a windmilling propeller. On a twin, live-engine thrust on one side and drag on the other give a strong yaw towards the dead engine, held with rudder. Climb performance drops by much more than half.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Yaw is towards the dead engine.

los.lo: Explain the reasons for feathering a propeller, including the effect on the yaw moment, performance and controllability.
los.title: Why feather
los.html:
Theory & physics

Feathering stops the propeller edge-on with minimum drag: smaller yawing moment (less rudder, lower VMC), better climb, better control, and no further damage to the failing engine.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Feathering reduces VMC.

topics.title: Propeller design characteristics that increase power absorption

los.lo: Name the propeller design characteristics that increase power absorption.
los.title: Increasing power absorption
los.html:
Theory & physics

Absorption rises with diameter, number of blades, blade chord, blade angle/camber and rpm.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • More blades = more power without more diameter.

los.lo: Explain the reasons for restricting propeller diameter.
los.title: Limits on propeller diameter
los.html:
Theory & physics

Tip speed: tips must stay well below Mach 1 (compressibility losses, noise). Ground clearance: at rotation, with a flat tyre or compressed oleo; plus clearance from fuselage and other propeller.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Two limits: tip speed and clearance.

los.lo: Define ‘solidity’.
los.title: Solidity
los.html:
Theory & physics

Solidity = total blade area ÷ propeller disc area.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • More or wider blades = higher solidity.

los.lo: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of increasing the number of blades.
los.title: More blades: pros and cons
los.html:
Theory & physics

Pros: absorb more power with smaller diameter (lower tip speed, less noise, more clearance), smoother, less vibration. Cons: weight, cost, complexity, slight efficiency loss (each blade works in the previous blade's disturbed air).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Efficiency per blade decreases.

los.lo: Describe how propeller noise can be minimised.
los.title: Reducing propeller noise
los.html:
Theory & physics

Lower tip speed (less rpm or diameter), more blades, swept/scimitar tips, and synchronising/synchrophasing propellers.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Noise is mostly a tip speed problem.

los.lo: Describe the effects of engine/propeller torque.
los.title: Torque reaction
los.html:
Theory & physics

(Clockwise from behind.) The propeller turns clockwise, so the aircraft rolls left (Newton 3). On the ground the left wheel is loaded more, adding to the swing; in flight it is trimmed or held with aileron.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Clockwise prop → roll left.

los.lo: Describe the following methods for counteracting engine/propeller torque: counter-rotating propellers; contra-rotating propellers.
los.title: Counter- and contra-rotating propellers
los.html:
Theory & physics

Counter-rotating: on a twin, engines turn opposite ways, cancelling torque and P-factor: no critical engine. Contra-rotating: two propellers on one axis turning opposite ways, cancelling torque, gyroscopic effect and swirl.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Counter = two engines; contra = one shaft.

los.lo: Describe what causes gyroscopic precession.
los.title: Gyroscopic precession
los.html:
Theory & physics

A spinning propeller is a gyroscope: a force on its rim acts 90° further round in the direction of rotation.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Precession = 90° in the direction of rotation.

los.lo: Describe the effect on the aeroplane due to the gyroscopic effect.
los.title: Gyroscopic effect on the aircraft
los.html:
Theory & physics

(Clockwise from behind.) Pitch down → yaw left (e.g. raising a tailwheel aircraft's tail); pitch up → yaw right; yaw left → pitch up; yaw right → pitch down. Strongest with large, heavy props and rapid attitude changes.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Tail-up on take-off roll → left yaw.

los.lo: Describe the possible effects of the rotating propeller slipstream.
los.title: Slipstream effects
los.html:
Theory & physics

The slipstream spirals round the fuselage in the propeller's direction; with a clockwise prop it hits the left side of the fin, yawing left. It also speeds the air over the tail and inner wing (better control and lift at low speed, high power) and can give asymmetric wing lift.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Slipstream swirl → yaw left (clockwise prop).

los.lo: Explain the asymmetric blade effect (also called P factor).
los.title: Asymmetric blade effect (P-factor)
los.html:
Theory & physics

With the propeller axis inclined to the flight path (high α, low speed), the descending blade has a larger α and higher speed and produces more thrust. With a clockwise prop the thrust centre moves right, yawing left.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Descending blade = more thrust.

los.lo: Explain the influence of direction of rotation on the critical engine on twin-engine aeroplanes.
los.title: Rotation direction and the critical engine
los.html:
Theory & physics

Both props clockwise from behind: descending blades on the right of each engine, so the right engine's thrust line is further from the centreline. Losing the left engine leaves the longer-armed thrust: the left engine is critical.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Clockwise props → left engine critical.

los.lo: Describe, given direction of propeller rotation, the propeller effects during take-off run, rotation and initial climb, and their consequence on controllability.
los.title: Propeller effects on take-off
los.html:
Theory & physics

(Clockwise.) Take-off run: torque (left wheel loading) and slipstream swing left; tailwheel: raising the tail adds gyroscopic left yaw. Rotation and initial climb: P-factor adds left yaw. Hold straight with right rudder, more at high power and low speed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • All effects yaw left → right rudder.

los.lo: Describe, given the direction of propeller rotation, the propeller effects during a go-around and their consequence on controllability.
los.title: Propeller effects in a go-around
los.html:
Theory & physics

Full power applied suddenly at low speed, nose rising: torque, slipstream and P-factor strengthen at once → strong left yaw and roll (clockwise) and nose-up pitch, while controls are least effective. Anticipate with rudder and pitch.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Go-around: sudden left yaw + pitch-up.

los.lo: Explain how propeller effects during go-around can be affected by: high engine performance conditions and their effect on the VMC speeds; loss of the critical engine; crosswind; high flap setting.
los.title: What worsens go-around propeller effects
los.html:
Theory & physics

High engine performance (low altitude, cold, dense air): more yaw and higher VMC. Loss of the critical engine mid go-around: largest asymmetry. Crosswind: adds to or reduces yaw via weathercocking. High flap: slow, draggy, more slipstream over flaps, weaker controls.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Cold, dense air → higher VMC.

los.lo: Describe the forces that act on an aeroplane in straight, horizontal, and steady flight.
los.title: Forces in straight and level flight
los.html:
Theory & physics

In straight, horizontal, steady flight there is no acceleration, so all forces (and moments) balance.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Steady = unaccelerated, not "lift greater than weight".

los.lo: List the four forces and state where they act on.
los.title: The four forces and where they act
los.html:
Theory & physics

Lift: perpendicular to the flight path, through the wing's CP. Weight: vertically down through the CG. Thrust: along the engines' thrust line. Drag: opposite the flight path, through a centre of drag.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Weight always acts through the CG.

los.lo: Explain how the four forces are balanced, including the function of the tailplane.
los.title: Balancing the four forces
los.html:
Theory & physics

Lift = weight, thrust = drag. Because they act at different points they also create pitching moments; the tailplane (usually a down-load) brings the sum of moments to zero, so the wing lifts slightly more than the weight.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Tail down-load → wing lift > weight in level flight.

los.lo: Define ‘flight-path angle’ (gamma).
los.title: Flight-path angle
los.html:
Theory & physics

γ (gamma) is the angle between the flight path and the horizontal.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • γ = climb (or descent) angle.

los.lo: Describe the relationship between pitch attitude, gamma and alpha for zero-wind and zero-bank conditions.
los.title: Pitch attitude, γ and α
los.html:
Theory & physics

With no wind and no bank: pitch attitude = γ + α.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Level flight: attitude = α.

los.lo: Describe the forces that act on an aeroplane in a straight, steady climb.
los.title: Forces in a steady climb
los.html:
Theory & physics

Weight is no longer perpendicular to the path: it splits into W sin γ (backwards along the path) and W cos γ (perpendicular to it).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • W sin γ is the extra "drag" of climbing.

los.lo: Name the forces parallel and perpendicular to the direction of flight. Apply the formula relating to the parallel forces (T equals D plus W sin gamma). Apply the formula relating to the perpendicular forces (L equals W cos gamma).
los.title: Climb force equations
los.html:
Theory & physics

Parallel: T = D + W sin γ. Perpendicular: L = W cos γ.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Climb: thrust carries drag plus part of the weight.

los.lo: Explain why thrust is greater than drag.
los.title: Why thrust exceeds drag in a climb
los.html:
Theory & physics

Thrust must overcome drag and lift part of the weight up the slope (W sin γ).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • T − D = W sin γ.

los.lo: Explain why lift is less than weight.
los.title: Why lift is less than weight in a climb
los.html:
Theory & physics

L = W cos γ, and cos γ < 1: part of the weight is carried by the thrust along the path.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Climb: L < W.

los.lo: Explain the formula (for small angles) that gives the relationship between gamma, thrust, weight, and lift-drag ratio, and use this formula for simple calculations.
los.title: Climb gradient formula
los.html:
Theory & physics

sin γ = (T − D)/W ≈ T/W − 1/(L/D): gradient depends on excess thrust per unit weight. Example: W 500 kN, T 100 kN, L/D 12 → ≈ 11.7 %; halve the thrust → ≈ 1.7 %.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Losing half the thrust cuts the gradient by far more than half.
  • Gradient depends on thrust, rate of climb on power.

los.lo: Explain how IAS, alpha, and gamma change in a climb performed with constant vertical speed and constant thrust setting.
los.title: Constant V/S climb at constant thrust
los.html:
Theory & physics

Thrust available falls with altitude, so excess thrust falls; holding the vertical speed uses kinetic energy: IAS falls, α rises, γ increases (RoC = TAS × sin γ, with TAS falling). Left alone, the speed decays towards the stall.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • V/S mode at altitude → speed decay.

los.lo: Describe the forces that act on an aeroplane in a straight, steady descent.
los.title: Forces in a steady powered descent
los.html:
Theory & physics

In a descent W sin γ acts forwards along the path, helping thrust.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Gravity helps pull the aircraft along.

los.lo: Name the forces parallel and perpendicular to the direction of flight. Apply the formula for forces parallel to the direction of flight (T equals D - W sin gamma). Apply the formula relating to the perpendicular forces (L equals W cos gamma).
los.title: Descent force equations
los.html:
Theory & physics

Parallel: T = D − W sin γ. Perpendicular: L = W cos γ.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Note the minus sign.

los.lo: Explain why lift is less than weight.
los.title: Why lift is less than weight in a descent
los.html:
Theory & physics

As in the climb, L = W cos γ < W because weight is tilted relative to the path.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • L < W in both climb and descent.

los.lo: Explain why thrust is less than drag.
los.title: Why thrust is less than drag in a descent
los.html:
Theory & physics

Part of the weight (W sin γ) helps pull the aircraft along, so less thrust is needed than drag.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Descent: T < D.

los.lo: Describe the forces that act on an aeroplane in a straight, steady glide.
los.title: Forces in a steady glide
los.html:
Theory & physics

No thrust: lift, drag and weight only. The forward weight component balances drag.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Gravity is the "engine".

los.lo: Name the forces parallel and perpendicular to the direction of flight. Apply the formula for forces parallel to the direction of flight (D equals W sin gamma). Apply the formula for forces perpendicular to the direction of flight (L equals W cos gamma).
los.title: Glide force equations
los.html:
Theory & physics

Parallel: D = W sin γ. Perpendicular: L = W cos γ.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Divide them: tan γ = D/L.

los.lo: Describe the relationship between the glide gradient and the lift-drag ratio, and calculate glide range given: initial height; L-D ratio; glide speed and wind speed.
los.title: Glide gradient, L/D and range
los.html:
Theory & physics

tan γ = D/L: glide angle depends only on L/D. Still-air distance = height × L/D; with wind, multiply by GS/TAS. Example: 10 000 ft × 12 ≈ 19.7 NM; at 120 kt TAS into 20 kt headwind ≈ 16.4 NM.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Glide ratio = L/D.

los.lo: Define VMD (speed for minimum drag) and explain the relationship between alpha, VMD and the best lift-drag ratio.
los.title: VMD and the best glide
los.html:
Theory & physics

VMD is flown at the α for (L/D)max, giving the flattest glide and longest still-air distance.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Best glide angle = VMD.

los.lo: Explain the effect of wind component on glide angle, duration, and distance.
los.title: Wind and the glide
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wind does not change the glide angle through the air or the duration (same airspeed), but changes ground angle and distance: headwind steeper and shorter over the ground; tailwind flatter and longer.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Duration is unchanged by wind.

los.lo: Explain the effect of mass change on glide angle, duration, and distance, given that the aeroplane remains at either the same airspeed or at VMD.
los.title: Mass and the glide
los.html:
Theory & physics

(L/D)max doesn't change with mass. At each mass's VMD: same angle and distance, but VMD higher (∝ √W), so higher rate of descent and shorter duration. At the same airspeed as a lighter aircraft's VMD: the heavy one is below its own VMD, lower L/D → steeper, shorter glide.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Heavier at own VMD: same distance, less time.

los.lo: Explain the effect of configuration change on glide angle and duration.
los.title: Configuration and the glide
los.html:
Theory & physics

Gear, flaps, speed brakes or a windmilling propeller reduce L/D: steeper glide and, at a given speed, higher rate of descent and shorter duration.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Feathering improves glide range.

los.lo: Describe the relation between TAS, gradient of descent, and rate of descent.
los.title: TAS, gradient and rate of descent
los.html:
Theory & physics

Rate of descent = TAS × sin γ. Same gradient at higher TAS (higher altitude or weight) → higher rate of descent.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Gradient is an angle; rate is a speed.

los.lo: Define VMP (speed for minimum power) and describe that the minimum rate of descent in the glide will be at VMP, and explain the relationship of this speed to the optimum speed for minimum glide angle.
los.title: VMP and minimum rate of descent
los.html:
Theory & physics

VMP (minimum power required, ≈ 0.76 VMD) gives the minimum rate of descent in a glide: longest time aloft, not longest distance (that's VMD).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • VMP < VMD.
  • Endurance (glide) = VMP; range (glide) = VMD.

los.lo: Discuss when a pilot could elect to fly for minimum glide rate of descent or minimum glide angle, and why speed stability or headwinds/tailwinds may favour a speed that is faster or slower than the optimum airspeed in still air.
los.title: Choosing glide speed
los.html:
Theory & physics

VMD to reach the furthest point (e.g. a distant field). VMP to stay airborne longest (restart, thermal). Headwind: fly faster than VMD for best ground range; tailwind: slightly slower. In practice fly a little above VMD for speed stability.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Headwind → faster.

los.lo: Describe the forces that act on an aeroplane in a steady, coordinated turn.
los.title: Forces in a coordinated turn
los.html:
Theory & physics

Lift tilts by bank φ: L cos φ balances weight; L sin φ provides the centripetal force mV²/R.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Horizontal lift component turns the aircraft.

los.lo: Resolve the forces that act horizontally and vertically during a coordinated turn (tan phi equals V squared over gR).
los.title: Turn force equations
los.html:
Theory & physics

Vertical: L cos φ = W. Horizontal: L sin φ = mV²/R. Dividing: tan φ = V²/(gR).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • No mass in the result.

los.lo: Describe the difference between a coordinated and an uncoordinated turn, and describe how to correct an uncoordinated turn using turn and slip indicator or turn coordinator.
los.title: Coordinated and uncoordinated turns
los.html:
Theory & physics

Coordinated: no sideslip, ball centred. Slipping: too much bank for the rate (too little rudder) → ball inside. Skidding: too little bank (too much rudder) → ball outside. Correct with rudder towards the ball ("step on the ball") or adjust bank.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Slip = ball in; skid = ball out.

los.lo: Explain why the angle of bank is independent of mass, and that it only depends on TAS and radius of turn.
los.title: Bank angle is independent of mass
los.html:
Theory & physics

tan φ = V²/(gR) has no mass: for a given TAS and radius every aircraft needs the same bank. A heavier one gets its extra lift from a higher CL, not more bank.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Heavier → same bank, higher α.

los.lo: Resolve the forces to show that for a given angle of bank the radius of turn is determined solely by airspeed (tan phi equals V squared over gR).
los.title: Radius depends only on TAS (for a given bank)
los.html:
Theory & physics

R = V²/(g tan φ): at a given bank, radius depends only on TAS.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Radius ∝ TAS².

los.lo: Calculate the turn radius of a steady turn given TAS and angle of bank.
los.title: Turn radius calculation
los.html:
Theory & physics

R = V²/(g tan φ), V in m/s. Example: 200 kt (102.9 m/s), 30° → 102.9² / (9.81 × 0.577) ≈ 1870 m ≈ 1.0 NM; at 250 kt ≈ 1.6 NM.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Convert kt → m/s (× 0.5144).

los.lo: Explain the effects of bank angle on: load factor (LF equals 1 over cos phi); alpha; thrust; drag.
los.title: Bank angle effects
los.html:
Theory & physics

Load factor n = 1/cos φ (30° 1.15, 45° 1.41, 60° 2); α must rise at the same speed; drag rises (mainly induced, ∝ n²); so thrust needed rises or the aircraft slows.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • 60° bank: n = 2, induced drag ×4.

los.lo: Define ‘angular velocity’.
los.title: Angular velocity
los.html:
Theory & physics

Angular velocity is the rate at which an angle changes, in °/s or rad/s.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Rate, not angle.

los.lo: Define ‘rate of turn’ and ‘rate-1 turn’.
los.title: Rate of turn and rate 1
los.html:
Theory & physics

Rate of turn = angular velocity of the heading change: ω = V/R = g tan φ / V. Rate 1 = 3°/s: 360° in 2 minutes.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Rate 1 = 3°/s.

los.lo: Explain the influence of TAS on rate of turn at a given bank angle.
los.title: TAS and rate of turn
los.html:
Theory & physics

At a given bank, higher TAS → lower rate of turn and larger radius. Rate-1 bank ≈ TAS/10 + 7 (150 kt ≈ 22°; 250 kt ≈ 32°).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Faster → more bank for rate 1.

los.lo: Calculate the load factor and stall speed in a turn given angle of bank and 1g stall speed.
los.title: Load factor and stall speed in a turn
los.html:
Theory & physics

n = 1/cos φ, VS turn = VS1G × √n. Example: 140 kt, 45° → n 1.41 → ≈ 166 kt.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Factor for 45°: × 1.19; for 60°: × 1.41.

los.lo: Explain situations in which turn radius is relevant for safety, such as maximum speed limits on departure or arrival plates, or outbound speed categories on approach plates, and the implications/hazards of exceeding given speeds.
los.title: Turn radius and safety
los.html:
Theory & physics

Departure/arrival maximum IAS and approach speed categories (A–E) exist because protected areas are sized for the turn radius at that speed. Flying faster makes the turn wider than the protected area → obstacles, terrain, traffic; worse at high airports (higher TAS for the IAS).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Speed limit on a SID protects the turn radius.

los.lo: Describe the hazards of excessive use of rudder to increase the rate of turn in a swept-wing aeroplane.
los.title: Rudder to tighten a turn in a swept-wing aircraft
los.html:
Theory & physics

Rudder creates sideslip; the swept wing's strong lateral stability turns it into a powerful roll, steepening the bank beyond control; large or reversing rudder can overload the fin. Turn with aileron, coordinate with minimum rudder.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Never "rudder" a swept-wing aircraft round a turn.

los.lo: Describe the effects on the aeroplane of asymmetric thrust during flight, for both jet-engined and propeller-driven aeroplanes.
los.title: Effects of asymmetric thrust
los.html:
Theory & physics

Live-engine thrust and dead-engine drag on opposite sides of the CG: yaw towards the dead engine; the live-side wing speeds up and (props) dead-side slipstream lift is lost → roll towards the dead engine → spiral if uncorrected. Drag rises (windmilling, sideslip, control deflection); climb performance falls far more than the thrust lost. Worse on propeller aircraft (slipstream loss, prop effects).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Yaw and roll toward the dead engine.

los.lo: Explain critical engine, and explain, for a propeller-driven aeroplane, the effect of the direction of propeller rotation.
los.title: Critical engine and propeller rotation
los.html:
Theory & physics

The critical engine is the one whose failure is most adverse for handling and performance. Twin props both clockwise from behind → left engine (P-factor moves the right engine's thrust line outboard). Identical jets: in principle none.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Counter-rotating props: no critical engine.

los.lo: Explain the effect of steady, asymmetric flight on a conventional (ball) slip indicator/turn indicator.
los.title: Slip indicator in asymmetric flight
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wings level, rudder only: ball centred but the aircraft sideslips towards the dead engine. Wings down (≈ 5° towards the live engine): zero sideslip, ball about half a width towards the live engine.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Centred ball ≠ zero sideslip with asymmetric thrust.

los.lo: Explain the effect of a crosswind on asymmetric flight.
los.title: Crosswind in asymmetric flight
los.html:
Theory & physics

A crosswind adds a weathercock yaw into wind. From the dead-engine side it adds to the yaw towards the dead engine and needs more rudder; from the live side it helps. On the ground it directly affects minimum control speed.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Worst case: crosswind from the dead-engine side.

topics.title: Balanced moments about the normal axis

los.lo: Explain the yaw moments about the CG.
los.title: Yaw moments about the CG
los.html:
Theory & physics

Live-engine thrust × arm plus dead-engine drag × arm, opposed by rudder/fin side force × fin arm and sideslip moments.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Balance: engine moments vs rudder moment.

los.lo: Explain the change to the yaw moment caused by the effect of air density on thrust.
los.title: Air density, thrust and yaw moment
los.html:
Theory & physics

Thrust depends on density: low altitude and low temperature give more thrust and a bigger yawing moment; high or hot, less.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Cold sea-level day = worst asymmetric yaw.

los.lo: Describe the changes to the yaw moment caused by engine distance from CG.
los.title: Engine distance from the CG
los.html:
Theory & physics

The further the engines from the CG (wide wing engines), the larger the yawing moment; engines close to the fuselage (rear-mounted) give less.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Rear-mounted engines → smaller asymmetric moment.

los.lo: Describe the methods to achieve directional balance following engine loss.
los.title: Restoring directional balance after engine loss
los.html:
Theory & physics

Rudder towards the live engine; bank up to 5° towards the live engine; feather (cut windmilling drag); if necessary reduce live-engine thrust; keep speed up (rudder power ∝ q).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • "Dead foot, dead engine": the idle foot is on the dead side.

topics.title: Forces parallel to the lateral axis

los.lo: Explain: the force on the vertical fin; the fuselage side force due to sideslip (using wing-level method); the use of bank angle to tilt the lift vector (in wing-down method).
los.title: Fin force, fuselage side force and bank
los.html:
Theory & physics

The fin/rudder side force holds the yaw. Wings level: balanced by a fuselage side force from sideslip (relative wind from the dead side) → fin α opposes the rudder → more rudder, more drag. Wings down (up to 5° toward live engine): tilted lift balances the fin force with no sideslip → less rudder, less drag, lower VMC.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Wings-down method gives the lower VMC.

los.lo: Explain the flight hazards at VMC: alpha; side slip; loads on the fin; alpha on the fin.
los.title: Hazards near VMC
los.html:
Theory & physics

High α near the stall (asymmetric stall → spin); sideslip adds drag and can hinder control; the fin at full rudder is highly loaded and its α can approach fin stall → sudden loss of directional control.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Near VMC: stall + asymmetry = spin risk.

los.lo: Explain the effect on fin alpha due to sideslip.
los.title: Sideslip and fin α
los.html:
Theory & physics

Wings level: sideslip from the dead side gives the fin an α against the rudder, so more rudder is needed. Sideslip the other way (too much bank toward the live engine) adds to fin α and, with full rudder, drives it towards fin stall.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Over-banking towards the live engine risks fin stall.

los.lo: Explain why controllability with one-engine-inoperative is a typical problem arising from the low speeds associated with low aeroplane mass.
los.title: Low mass and OEI controllability
los.html:
Theory & physics

Rudder power depends on speed (q); asymmetric thrust doesn't depend on mass. A light aircraft has low stall and take-off speeds, where the rudder may not balance full asymmetric thrust: VMC may limit V1, VR, V2 instead of the stall.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Light weight → VMC becomes limiting.

los.lo: Define ‘VMC’.
los.title: VMC
los.html:
Theory & physics

VMC (VMCA): the CAS at which, with the critical engine suddenly inoperative, control can be maintained and straight flight held with ≤ 5° bank towards the live engine.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Max 5° bank toward the live engine.

los.lo: Describe how VMC is determined.
los.title: How VMC is determined
los.html:
Theory & physics

Max take-off thrust on the live engine(s); most unfavourable (aft) CG; trimmed for take-off; take-off flaps; gear up; failed propeller in its normal condition (windmilling or auto-feathered); out of ground effect; most critical weight. Rudder force ≤ 150 lbf (667 N), heading change ≤ about 20°; VMC ≤ 1.13 VSR.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • 150 lbf rudder force limit.

los.lo: Explain the influence of the CG location.
los.title: CG and VMC
los.html:
Theory & physics

An aft CG shortens the rudder's arm → less yawing moment → higher VMC. Hence it is determined at the aft limit.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Aft CG = highest VMC.

topics.title: Minimum control speed during approach and landing (VMCL)

los.lo: Define ‘VMCL’.
los.title: VMCL
los.html:
Theory & physics

VMCL: the CAS at which, with the critical engine suddenly inoperative in the approach and landing configuration, control can be maintained with ≤ 5° bank.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • "L" = landing configuration.

los.lo: Describe how VMCL is determined.
los.title: How VMCL is determined
los.html:
Theory & physics

Landing configuration, trimmed for approach, go-around thrust on the live engine(s), failed propeller in its normal condition, most unfavourable weight and aft CG, with rudder force limits.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Uses go-around thrust.

los.lo: Explain the influence of the CG location.
los.title: CG and VMCL
los.html:
Theory & physics

Aft CG → shorter rudder arm → higher VMCL.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Same logic as VMC.

topics.title: Minimum control speed on the ground (VMCG)

los.lo: Define ‘VMCG’.
los.title: VMCG
los.html:
Theory & physics

VMCG: the CAS on the take-off run at which, with the critical engine suddenly inoperative, control can be kept with primary aerodynamic controls only (no nosewheel steering) and the take-off safely continued, deviating ≤ 30 ft (9.1 m) from the centreline.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • No nosewheel steering; 30 ft max deviation.

los.lo: Describe how VMCG is determined.
los.title: How VMCG is determined
los.html:
Theory & physics

Take-off thrust on the live engine(s), most critical take-off configuration, trimmed for take-off, most unfavourable (aft) CG and weight, rudder force ≤ 150 lbf. V1 ≥ VMCG.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • V1 may not be below VMCG.

los.lo: Explain the influence of the CG location.
los.title: CG and VMCG
los.html:
Theory & physics

Aft CG → shortest rudder arm → highest VMCG.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • All three VMC speeds are worst at aft CG.

los.lo: Describe the influence of density on thrust during asymmetric flight.
los.title: Density and thrust in asymmetric flight
los.html:
Theory & physics

Live-engine thrust is highest at low pressure altitude and low temperature (high density).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Dense air → more asymmetric thrust.

los.lo: Explain why VMC, VMCL and VMCG reduce with a reduction in thrust.
los.title: Why minimum control speeds fall with less thrust
los.html:
Theory & physics

Less thrust → less yawing moment → the rudder balances it at a lower dynamic pressure, so VMC, VMCL and VMCG decrease at high altitude, high temperature, or with derated thrust. Highest at low, cold airfields.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Hot and high → lower VMC.
  • Derated take-off thrust → lower VMCG → lower V1 possible.

subs.title: Significant points on a polar curve

los.lo: Identify and explain the significant points on a polar curve.
los.title: Significant points on the polar
los.html:
Theory & physics

CL = 0: zero lift, near CDmin. Tangent from origin: (CL/CD)max → VMD, best glide, jet max endurance. (CL3/2/CD)max (higher CL) → VMP, min rate of descent, prop max endurance. (CL1/2/CD)max (lower CL) → jet best range (≈ 1.32 VMD). CLMAX: the stall.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • VMP is at a higher CL (lower speed) than VMD.
